events.title: McKinsey: Cheaper AI models, bigger AI bills
events.summary: Good morning. Intelligence is getting radically cheaper, but enterprise AI bills keep climbing anyway. That was the central paradox McKinsey senior partners Tanguy Catlin and Lari Hämäläinen tackled on Tuesday during a McKinsey Live virtual session, “Improving the Economics of Agentic AI,” which highlighted the firm’s State of AI in 2026 survey. “Intelligence at a certain capability level is getting a lot more affordable,” said Hämäläinen, who is also a leader in McKinsey Digital. For example, GPT-4 launched in 2023, with the 8K-context API priced at $60 per million output tokens. Today, models that perform at roughly the same level as GPT-4 on established benchmarks can be run for a fraction of the cost—yet companies are still spending more and more on AI, he explained. But as the cost of producing a unit of intelligence collapses, the amount businesses consume is exploding. Models are getting cheaper per unit of capability while enterprises ask them to perform vastly more reasoning and work, especially through autonomous agents. AI vendors are also capturing some of those efficiency gains through higher margins, Hämäläinen said. In software development, for example, AI agents can repeatedly inspect, modify and rewrite entire codebases, generating far more code than a human developer would typically touch, he said. The economics of agentic AI Companies are only beginning to understand the economics of agentic AI, Hämäläinen said. Unlike traditional software, where the cost of running a task is relatively predictable, agents can take different paths to the same result, making costs highly variable. The same task can cost up to 30 times more from one run to another, he said. Much of that cost comes from the reasoning and repeated refinement behind the final output. System design matters: choices such as using a single agent versus multiple agents can dramatically affect the cost of completing a task, Hämäläinen said. AI cost management has become more about engineering systems that don’t waste tokens in the first place. Rather than measuring agents by cost per token, he said leaders should evaluate them at the task level: how much a task costs to execute, how often the agent succeeds, and how much human time is required to verify its work. As a rule of thumb, an agent can make sense when the time required to verify its output is a small fraction of the time it would take a human to complete the task from scratch, he said. If a task takes a human an hour, but an agent’s work can be verified in six minutes, an agent with a success rate above 10% could already begin to create value, he added. The bigger challenge, he said, is redesigning the surrounding workflow to take advantage of the capacity the agent frees up. Meanwhile, “The truth is, there is no single cost lever,” said Catlin, who is also a director of the McKinsey Global Institute. He identified three areas where companies can manage AI spending: —First, companies need visibility into which use cases, business units, agents, models and users are driving spend. —Second, they need to optimize workflows by matching model complexity to the task, routing requests to appropriate models, caching reusable context and limiting unnecessary tool calls and agent loops. —Third, they need greater sourcing discipline, including removing unused licenses, managing quotas, negotiating provider terms and avoiding excessive dependence on a single model or vendor. But Catlin cautioned that the goal should not be indiscriminate cost-cutting. Companies should determine where AI spending delivers the highest returns and optimize toward those returns. events.title: The Download: India’s smart glasses menace and AI’s trillion-dollar gamble
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Smart glasses are already causing havoc in India When Shubnam saw an Instagram video of a Delhi protest they had attended, they realized a content creator wearing Meta smart glasses had recorded them surreptitiously. The mocking reel drew millions of views, along with transphobic abuse and AI-generated memes. Experts warn that many others will experience similar ordeals as smart glasses go mainstream. The risks are particularly acute in India, where covert recording and the circulation of images without consent are already pervasive. The bigger issue is that the smart glasses aren’t just being used to turn ordinary people into targets of viral “pranks.” They’re also becoming a tool of police surveillance. Here’s why smart glasses are creating new privacy risks in India . —Anuj Behal MIT Technology Review Narrated: what’s at stake in AI’s trillion-dollar gamble When Jessica Wachter, a University of Pennsylvania finance professor, wanted to assess AI’s impact on the economy over the next few years, she started with a simple fact: a handful of so-called hyperscalers are investing huge amounts of money to build AI data centers. Instead of trying to predict how widely deployed AI models will be, Wachter asked how fast the hyperscalers’ earnings will need to grow to justify their spending through 2027, when expenditures are expected to reach nearly $1.1 trillion. The results are eye-opening. AI companies will need to achieve an extraordinary increase in productivity just to break even by 2030 . This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts . Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released. events.title: Royal Caribbean agrees to take 50% equity stake in Sandals for $3 billion
events.summary: Royal Caribbean has agreed to take a 50% equity stake in Sandals. The deal values Sandals at $6 billion. It deepens Royal Caribbean’s push into land-based vacations. Royal Caribbean has agreed to take a 50% equity stake in Sandals for $3 billion, the companies announced Wednesday. The deal values the Caribbean resort chain at $6 billion and is expected to boost growth for both companies. The transaction is expected to close early next year. Royal Caribbean's stock is down roughly 25% over the past year after it trimmed its forecasts for revenue growth on softer demand for European sailings. The cruise company has been intent on diversifying beyond cruises and becoming a leader in vacations overall. Royal Caribbean already operates several private destinations for its cruise passengers, but it has been working to build out its land offerings. Sandals and its Beaches brand, meanwhile, have more than a dozen properties across the Caribbean, giving Royal Caribbean a foothold in all-inclusive options. The Financial Times and CNBC earlier reported the companies were in talks.

events.title: Reddit is ramping up its war on marketing slop
events.summary: Adam Collins, Reddit's chief communications officer, wants to preserve the platform's human qualities. Reddit Reddit is ramping up its crackdown on marketing slop. It'll limit the distribution of suspected spam so it doesn't appear in the home feed. Reddit also found a big network that violated its rules requiring disclosure of marketing activity. Reddit is ratcheting up its war on marketing slop. The company exclusively told CMO Insider that it's taking new steps to combat spam and keep human conversations at the center of its platform. First, it'll prevent suspected spam from appearing in the main home feed while it's under review. Reddit said in testing, this approach cut spam in the home feed by 28%, user reports of spam in the feed by 11%, and push notifications with spam by 7%. It plans to test this approach in search results next. Reddit is also taking a few other steps: It plans to start explaining to users why it suspects certain content is spam, rather than just showing "Removed by Reddit" It won't recommend posts or comments from accounts that have been asked to verify they're human or register their automation, but haven't yet done so "What's made Reddit really unique over the last 21 years, and special, is the humanity that you see on Reddit every day," said Adam Collins, Reddit's chief communications officer. "Our goal is to preserve that for the future as well. That's really what these efforts are about." Reddit said it had uncovered a coordinated network of 485 accounts that created more than 44,000 pieces of content across the platform, often about work and productivity. These accounts presented themselves as regular users but were, in fact, connected to businesses, violating Reddit's rules requiring marketing activity to be disclosed. Reddit said it reversed the potential benefit of the coordinated behavior by removing karma and votes that resulted from the manipulation. Karma is a score on Reddit that measures a user's reputation. The spam problem is a particular threat to Reddit, which considers its human-moderated communities to be its greatest advantage over other social platforms. Reddit vs. AI After going public in 2024, Reddit increased advertising on its forums and entered into  partnerships with OpenAI and Google. Marketers took note and have been racing to create content for Reddit. Brands particularly hope their efforts will help them show up in AI search , where Reddit is highly cited. The problem: Self-promotional content from brands, especially if they use AI to make it, risks harming the human quality that Reddit sees as setting itself apart from other platforms. A July report from the AI detection firm Pangram found that Reddit was the least affected by AI among five platforms, with 3% of its short-form content flagged as AI. LinkedIn was at the high end at 30%. Reddit has been proactive. In July, Reddit announced tools to combat AI-enabled promotional content and spam. Reddit said at the time that these tools helped catch 23 million spam views per day and cut users' exposure to spam by about 20% in the period from January to March 2026, compared to the prior three months. Collins said that while some commercial spam is obvious to users, these tools were able to catch subtler instances, such as spam accounts that appeared to be people interacting with each other. Moderation is an ongoing Whac-A-Mole game, though, and as long as spammers keep finding workarounds, Reddit's work will continue. "The conversations that are happening on Reddit have value," Collins said. "We have to continue to adjust and continue to improve our efforts to remove that kind of content to make sure that it continues to be that great value of a place for users." What marketers are saying Agency execs who spoke with CMO Insider said brands that use Reddit as intended — by listening to their consumers and being useful to them — won't be affected by the spam crackdown. "The brands that win will earn participation by being transparent, useful, and native to each community, while giving customers genuine reasons to talk about them," said Joe Gagliese, co-CEO of Viral Nation. Brian Yamada, chief innovation officer at VML, said the sugar rush some brands got by manipulating Reddit would be short-lived. Slop isn't going away, though, he added. "It's not just a Reddit problem," Yamada said. "The flood of generative AI slop is likely to continue as brands or companies are looking for shortcuts or cheats to get visible." Collins said Reddit has an appeals process to correct false positives and that it's letting suspected spam remain while it's under review. Moderators and users play an important gatekeeping role on Reddit, and Collins said that wouldn't change. Moderators can still review and approve content for their communities, but limiting suspected spam during a review period would help prevent users from being exposed to it, he said. events.title: Adtech vet Brian O'Kelley's startup is pivoting to AI agents and rebranding with a new name
events.summary: Apostra cofounders Brian O'Kelley and Anne Coghlan Franco Vogt Pivot! Adtech veteran Brian O'Kelley's Scope3 startup is rebranding. Apostra wants to become a leader in agentic AI advertising. The startup acts as an "orchestration layer" connecting advertiser agents with publisher agents. Adtech veteran Brian O'Kelley , once described as the "master of the hard pivot," is pushing the reset button again. O'Kelley and his cofounder, Anne Coghlan, exclusively told CMO Insider that they are renaming their company from Scope3 to Apostra as they aim to make the startup a leader in agentic AI advertising. They describe Apostra as a platform that connects advertisers' AI agents with AI agents representing media sellers, so that marketers don't have to build separate integrations with potentially thousands of publishers, platforms, and other media providers. O'Kelley told CMO Insider that advertising has been constrained by a fragmented media infrastructure, manual processes, and a programmatic advertising landscape organized around real-time bidding but not optimized for the most highly valued ad placements. "You can't buy anything that's not a rectangle with a cookie," O'Kelley said. Apostra is designed to let AI agents handle the work of negotiating and managing ad campaigns across various publishers, including online placements, linear TV, and in-store audio, and to connect brands with creators and clippers. The advertiser agent makes the media owner's agent aware of the marketer's goals, while the media owner's agent can bring forward details about the publisher's audience and potential ad opportunities. Apostra uses AdCP, a protocol created last year by a consortium of adtech companies, including Scope3, that provides a common language for agents to interact. Apostra said this makes it easier for marketers to place ads in channels such as "walled garden" social platforms , podcasts, or out-of-home advertising, which are traditionally harder to reach through programmatic ad buying. Unlike traditional programmatic advertising , this doesn't involve software bidding on individual ad impressions in real time. Instead, the agents can automate parts of the slower process of discovering, negotiating, approving, and executing media deals. The company says it's working with 40 media partners and has built AdCP adapters for major ad platforms, including Google, Meta, Amazon, Reddit, and ChatGPT Ads. Apostra said it is already running seven-figure campaigns through the system. O'Kelley said an unnamed major brand began with a $1 million US campaign in April, then expanded the experiment into several other markets and channels. While it may sound like an ad network, Apostra said it functions more like a neutral gateway. It doesn't charge transaction fees or a percentage of media spend like other adtech platforms, but will instead sell add-on "intelligence capabilities" such as campaign proposal evaluation, negotiation support, catalog integration, and currency handling. Apostra says that by using its technology, marketers could discover media they wouldn't otherwise access through traditional sales channels, and publishers could gain access to more advertiser demand and reduce the costs of selling ad space. The process isn't necessarily fully autonomous. Publishers can still require human approval for campaigns, while brands can retain control over things like how the creative looks and the broader strategy. O'Kelley gave the example of a media partner whose AI agent posts proposed ads to a Slack channel for a human employee to review. 'Master of the hard pivot' The launch of Apostra marks another twist in O'Kelley's long adtech career. O'Kelley was credited with helping to invent the ad exchange at the adtech startup Right Media, which sold to Yahoo shortly after he left the company. O'Kelley was fired from his chief technology role there after telling the Right Media board not to take the deal. O'Kelley, sometimes referred to in the trade press as the "godfather of adtech," went on to launch the adtech company AppNexus , which sold to AT&T for a reported $1.6 billion in 2018. Scope3 has a complicated founding story. In 2019, O'Kelley cofounded a company called CMDTY, which later changed its name to Waybridge and operated a supply-chain platform that tracked the movement of raw materials. He began Scope3 as a side project, offering a service that let advertisers, agencies, and publishers measure the carbon impact of their digital advertising. Waybridge returned some of its $30 million Series B funding to its investors, who in turn reinvested $20 million from a seed round in Scope3 . Scope3 had raised $60 million in total , O'Kelley said. He told CMO Insider that he had been planning to expand the company beyond carbon tracking since as far back as 2022. The turning point was 2025, as companies began scaling back their sustainability programs, he said. He added that, until then, the company had been "doubling" revenue each year. The company decided to put all of its focus into the Apostra project "when it became clear the sustainability business wasn't going to double," O'Kelley said. Scope3 launched its agentic media platform in March 2025. The agent-to-agent tool was designed to execute media transactions and root out inefficiencies in the programmatic ad buying space. Scope3 helped launch AdCP in October. Joseph Hirsch, CEO of the adtech company Swivel, dubbed O'Kelley the " master of the hard pivot " last year while describing O'Kelley's reimagining of the programmatic ad landscape as a system dominated by agents. Others in the industry have been more critical of O'Kelley's serial reinvention. In covering Scope3's divestment this year of Adloox, an ad verification startup it had acquired a couple of years previously, trade publication AdtechRadar said Scope3 continued "to shift its strategy as it searches for a durable growth story." O'Kelley said the launch of Apostra is the company's "burn the boats" moment. The company had two rounds of layoffs over the past year and has reduced its head count from over 100 staffers to about 40 people. "It's just really hard to make money in programmatic when your future vision is to kill programmatic," O'Kelley said. The jury's still out on how quickly marketers will adopt agentic advertising, or whether it will achieve the scale its proponents envision. Procurement processes at large brands often lag new trends. Many ad buying decisions are built on the strength of old-fashioned, human relationships and dealmaking — hence the longevity of events like the annual US TV upfronts . events.title: Legal AI startup Spellbook hired a new CMO — and she has strong opinions on avoiding 'creepy' AI marketing
events.summary: Meltem Kuran-Berkowitz has joined Spellbook as its chief marketing officer. Meltem Kuran Berkowitz Legal AI startup Spellbook has appointed Meltem Kuran-Berkowitz as its CMO. Kuran-Berkowitz wants Spellbook's marketing to help it hit the $100 million mark. Spellbook is embracing AI, but she draws the line at using it to impersonate human communication. The new CMO of a legal tech startup has a message for marketers: Stop using AI to pretend to be human. Spellbook, which offers AI tools for drafting and analyzing legal contracts, exclusively told CMO Insider that it had appointed Meltem Kuran-Berkowitz as its chief marketing officer. She is taking the top marketing role full time after a brief stint freelancing for the company. Kuran-Berkowitz previously spent five and a half years as head of growth at the payroll and workforce platform Deel, overseeing the company's growth to $1 billion in annual recurring revenue. Kuran-Berkowitz joins Spellbook as it, too, is leveling up. In October 2025, the company raised $50 million in Series B funding at a $350 million valuation, led by Khosla Ventures. In March, the company secured a $40 million debt facility, which it said it would put toward acquiring rival generative AI companies. The legal tech space is booming. Investors poured $2 billion into startups building for the legal sector in the first half of this year, per the market research firm Crunchbase, as AI has transformed one of Silicon Valley's sleepier corners into one of its hottest. Legal AI specialists like Harvey and Legora are competing alongside tech giants like OpenAI as law firms and corporate legal teams race to adopt tools that promise to automate grunt work. Kuran-Berkowitz said an early measure of her success will be helping the company hit $100 million in revenue by the end of this year. Getting there, she said, means making far more potential customers aware of the company. She doesn't plan to flood them with AI-generated marketing, though. "If we're going to get somebody's eyeballs, whether it's in an email or an Instagram post, we're going to be honest with you about it: it's going to be made from another human, and we're not going to waste your time," Kuran-Berkowitz said. There are places where Kuran-Berkowitz thinks AI can be useful in marketing, from mining sales calls for insights to building internal presentation decks . She draws the line when it starts to impersonate human interaction. "My inbox has blown out with cold emails because now everybody can write them. Now, everybody finds the one niche thing we have in common," Kuran-Berkowitz said. She gave the example of AI-personalized cold emails that manufacture tenuous connections with lines like: "I was in Italy once." She said that kind of AI-generated familiarity "feels creepy." "I feel very strongly towards those things, and I just don't want to do that to people," Kuran-Berkowitz said. Spellbook CEO Scott Stevenson also has strong opinions on his employees' use of AI. Earlier this month, he wrote a memo encouraging staffers to write the rough, " D+ version " of their ideas first, before leaning on AI to polish their proposals. Spellbook's marketing plan Kuran-Berkowitz said she doesn't want to follow legal tech startups like Harvey and Legora in going down the celebrity-sponsorship marketing route. Instead, she wants "every single touchpoint with the customer to be meaningful," and explain what the product does. Her media strategy involves showing up in the places where Spellbook's potential customers already spend their time — from closed communities to newsletters — without, as Kuran-Berkowitz puts it, "ruining the vibes." "Where can we fit ourselves nicely without ruining the vibes? And then what can we produce and add to the vibes?" she said. This summer, for example, Spellbook created a $1 million fellowship fund for law students to help them streamline wonky legal workflows. Ultimately, Kuran-Berkowitz wants to expand perceptions of Spellbook beyond the redlining tool that made its name. She wants Spellbook to be the default brand people associate with managing contracts. "The world runs on contracts," she said. "That's just a fact, and the contracts run on Spellbook." events.title: Ema raises $77M as AI starts eating into enterprise software and services
events.summary: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now Disrupt ticket savings of up to $200 + 50% off a second ends Sept 25, 11:59 p.m. PT. REGISTER HERE. Ema , a startup that uses teams of AI agents to automate corporate processes across HR, IT, and finance, has raised $77 million in a new funding round as it aims to take on more of the work traditionally handled by enterprise software and IT services. The Series B round was led by Bengaluru-based venture firm Creaegis, with existing investors Accel, Section 32, and Prosus increasing their stakes. The financing brings the startup’s total funding to $140 million and more than quadruples its valuation from its last funding round in 2024. (Ema declined to disclose its latest valuation.) The round consisted entirely of primary equity, with no debt or secondary transactions, the startup confirmed to TechCrunch. The funding comes as AI is beginning to compete for dollars that businesses have traditionally spent on enterprise software and IT services. Startups, major AI labs, and established software companies are now fighting to capture that spending. Founded in 2023 by former Google and Coinbase executive Surojit Chatterjee and ex-Okta executive Souvik Sen, Ema is looking to expand its position in that market. The startup deploys its technology, which it calls “AI employees” — systems that coordinate multiple AI agents. These help carry out multi-step business processes across a company’s existing applications, rather than handling a single task at a time. Chatterjee sees that model eventually reducing companies’ reliance on traditional software products, including those sold as software-as-a-service (SaaS). Ema first “wraps” around an enterprise’s existing applications, he said, before customers can reduce their dependence on some of those products — and, in some cases, replace them altogether. “Many of our customers are already on the way to replace [large SaaS applications] completely, removing dependency on them, because they are mostly becoming like a database,” Chatterjee said. In recent months, major AI companies have also pushed deeper into the enterprise market where Ema operates. Anthropic has expanded efforts to bring Claude into companies’ core operations, including financial and legal work. Similarly, OpenAI has established teams of forward-deployed engineers who work alongside customers to put AI into production. Chatterjee, however, does not see the frontier AI labs as direct competitors. He told TechCrunch that Ema’s software can draw on more than 150 models, including frontier and open source models, while the startup focuses on the domain knowledge, integrations, and orchestration needed to automate business processes end-to-end. “Progress in frontier models is actually very beneficial to us,” Chatterjee stated. Ema’s approach is already gaining traction. The startup has more than 50 active enterprise deals, as well as over 1 million active enterprise users, and has handled more than 5 million actions and queries. Its customers include NTT DATA, Hitachi, ADP, PwC, Google, KPMG, Wipro, and Microsoft. Over the past two years, Ema said its revenue has grown 50-fold, while revenue bookings have surpassed $150 million. Chatterjee said the bookings figure includes the total value of multiyear contracts, including two- and three-year deals, rather than representing annual recurring revenue. He, however, declined to disclose the startup’s current annualized revenue run rate. Chatterjee told TechCrunch that more than 90% of Ema’s customers have expanded beyond their initial use case, with some deploying the technology across dozens of workflows. The startup’s net dollar retention rate is around 180%, he said, meaning existing customers are spending substantially more with Ema over time. Ema is also looking beyond the software itself. AI, Chatterjee said, can take over some of the implementation, integration, and consulting work that companies have traditionally paid IT services firms to perform around enterprise software. “A lot of the services companies are working with us,” Chatterjee said. “They are also dramatically changing or disrupting their own business models because they understand the human-forward model may not be the best model going forward.” Despite taking on work traditionally handled by software and services providers, Chatterjee said Ema has maintained gross margins of close to 80%. The startup, he noted, requires less human support as its AI systems learn from deployments, helping improve margins over time. Ema also does not charge customers based on software seats or the number of AI tokens they consume. Instead, Chatterjee said, its pricing is tied to the completion of tasks and business outcomes. Much of Ema’s new capital will go toward expanding its go-to-market operations, particularly sales and marketing, after spending its first years largely building the product, Chatterjee said.

events.title: Pornhub investigated over concerns it can still be accessed by UK children
events.summary: Watchdog Ofcom says site’s age-checking regime may not be ‘highly effective’, as required by the Online Safety Act One of the world’s most visited pornography websites is being investigated by the UK’s communications watchdog over concerns it can still be accessed by children. Pornhub’s age checking regime may not be “highly effective”, according to Ofcom , and could be in breach of online safety laws requiring strict measures to prevent under-18s from accessing sexually explicit content. Ofcom is investigating Pornhub’s use of Apple’s age verification process to determine whether someone is the appropriate age for viewing pornography. Pornhub had blocked access to new UK users in response to the Online Safety Act , but announced in May it would use so-called device-level checks, meaning users in the UK who had confirmed they were 18 or older through Apple’s age-verification process would be able to access Pornhub and be “served a standard adult user experience”. Ofcom raised concerns over that decision on Wednesday. Announcing the investigation, it said the act was “clear that it is the service provider’s responsibility to ensure that any age assurance process is highly effective – no matter at what stage an age check occurs”. The regulator added: “We are concerned that Aylo [Pornhub’s owner] may not have conducted sufficient due diligence and testing before implementing its new age assurance process. “As a result, we are concerned that Aylo’s process may not be highly effective at preventing children from seeing pornography.” Ofcom said its investigation was not focusing on Apple’s age checks specifically, but on whether Pornhub owner Aylo’s reliance on that system was in line with the act – because it is the content provider’s responsibility to ensure whether its age-checking measures are robust or not. Some Ofcom checks of Aylo’s device-level checking system have shown the website could have been accessed by children. George Lusty, Ofcom’s director of enforcement, said: “Online age checks are a vital protection to prevent children from encountering inappropriate or harmful material, including pornography. “We expect tech firms to ensure age checks are highly effective before introducing them. Anything less could leave children at risk.” A finding that Aylo broke the law could result in a fine of up to £18m or 10% of the company’s global revenue, whichever is greater. Beeban Kidron, a crossbench peer and prominent campaigner for child internet safety, said she hoped the Ofcom investigation would result in a renewed drive for effective age checking. “Extremely effective privacy preserving age assurance has been possible for years. It is a question of corporate priorities. I hope the action by Ofcom pushes it up the priority list not only at Pornhub but accross the sector,” she said. In July, Ofcom said there had been “significant progress” in implementing age checks across tech platforms in pornography, social media, dating and gaming. It said the proportion of children who encountered highly effective age checks increased from 25% to 43% between July 2025 and January this year. It added that a minority of children (8%) had attempted to access pornography, and half of them reached sites with age checks in place. Nonetheless, it said “more action is needed” on age checking, particularly with an under-16 social media ban being implemented next year .

events.title: Legal & General to cut 1,000 jobs by mid-2027
events.summary: Programme will initially involve voluntary redundancies in the UK but the insurance and pensions firm will consider mandatory job cuts depending on the take-up Legal & General plans to cut 1,000 jobs by the middle of next year, about a tenth of the British insurance and pensions firm’s workforce. António Simões, the chief executive, is wielding the axe as part of his attempts to create a “leaner organisation” since taking over from longtime CEO Nigel Wilson in January 2024. L&G described the move as “the next stage of that transformation”. The London-headquartered firm told staff on Wednesday that it had begun moves to eliminate about 1,000 roles by mid-2027, which had first been reported by Bloomberg News. Most of L&G’s 10,000 employees are based in the UK. The programme will initially involve voluntary redundancies in the UK but L&G will consider mandatory job cuts depending on the take-up. The fund management division, which oversees £1.2tn in assets, is excluded as it has its own restructuring plan. Simões, who previously worked for Santander and HSBC, announced a sharper focus on L&G’s booming pensions arm in June 2024 and reduced the group’s four businesses to three, by merging its asset management divisions. It sold several “non-strategic” assets, the biggest of which was the housebuilder Cala Homes, along with legacy land and real estate. He also brought in a new executive team and pledged to return more than £5bn to shareholders between 2025 and 2027 through dividends and share buybacks. Simões told employees in an email: “Over the past two-and-a-half years, we have made significant progress executing our strategy, simplifying L&G, establishing three core businesses, and creating a more focused business. “However, over the last decade, different structures, processes and ways of working have developed across L&G, making us more complex than we need to be… we need to change how we work today and, through this, become a leaner organisation.” An L&G spokesperson said the changes “will help us focus our resources and investment on the areas where we see the strongest opportunities for long-term growth”. The spokesperson added: “We recognise and take seriously the impact on colleagues and are committed to supporting our people throughout the process and consulting with our unions.” The company expects £500bn of transactions in the UK pensions market over the next decade, as employers transfer their old defined benefit pension plans to insurers and pension companies. L&G said it was also benefiting from strong auto-enrolment of staff in their companies’ pension schemes, with about £1bn of new inflows each month.

events.title: Meta's Muse reignites AI disruption fears. Traders are targeting this brokerage stock as next casualty
events.summary: Meta's latest consumer AI product is sending such big shockwaves through the market that it's even inflaming a long-time rivalry in the brokerage business between 55-year old investing giant Charles Schwab , and Robinhood , an icon of the post-Covid trading boom among young investors. Shares of Schwab fell 6% Tuesday, touching the lowest since early July and the stock is now down more than 8% since Meta announced Muse. Meanwhile, Robinhood's stock was higher, notching anotheryear-to-date high. In May, the company launched AI agents that can now trade and manage portfolios on behalf of users. Shares of sprawling wealth management business LPL Financial Holdings dropped 7% Tuesday, financial services firm Raymond James Financial shed 3.5 percent, and Interactive Brokers slipped 1% as the State Street Financial Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLF) lost 2% and is now down 6 percent from highs made earlier this month. Higher interest rates may not be helping. It's not the first time an AI product has jostled the group – in February, the same group of stocks dropped when tech platform Altruist said its platform `Hazel' can create tax-planning strategies for individuals and advisors. Schwab stock recovered some in the months after – LPL has not. "Schwab's an interesting animal," said Jimmy Lee, founder and CEO of The Wealth Consulting Group, a Las Vegas-based advisor that oversees $8 billion in assets. "To us in the advisor space they're kind of neutral and figuring out how best to protect their market share. I don't think Meta brings a lot of competition from the custodian perspective because it's not like Altruist's platform, but there is a lot of disruption that's going to happen among financial middle-men that charge fees for billing, reporting, trading, etc." Meta's AI assistant says it won't trade for users or give financial advice, but when queried with how it might mimic the work of a financial advisor or broker, lists abilities including tracking investments and progress towards goals, as well as analyzing how portfolio holdings fit together. Last week, Schwab Advisor Services, the company's platform for registered investment advisors, announced it is working with Anthropic to create Claude for Financial Advisors. In May, the company launched an AI tool that includes tailored analysis from the company's research arm. Representatives from Schwab did not respond to a request for comment. Robinhood reps declined to add to this story. Robinhood's bounce on Tuesday brings its stock to a 10% rally on the year after dropping more than 40% in the first three months. The retail-focused brokerage, which also offers digital banking and advisory services, is up 1200 percent the past three years. Schwab stock is up 83 percent and the XLF is up 65 percent. "AI and tokenization threaten to dismantle the frictions that legacy financial intermediaries have historically monetized," Piper Sandler analyst Patrick Moley wrote in a note in April. "Schwab's reliance on low-yielding sweep cash puts it squarely in the crosshairs." Judging by options-market flows around the stocks on Tuesday, the threat to Schwab may be a lasting one. Options volume in Schwab was more than five times the average, with nearly twice as many puts bought vs. calls, Cboe LiveVol data show. The most popular contract to buy was the 90-strike put expiring mid-January, a bet the stock drops another 13% the next three months. To be sure, there was one big counter-trade sale of the Oct. 16 95-strike puts. What's arguably most notable is in Robinhood options, sentiment was the opposite – traders bought twice as many calls as puts with more than 80 percent of the $95 million in premium traded tied to calls. The most heavily traded contract was the 125-strike call expiring on Friday. "Gen Z and millennials gravitate towards platforms like Robinhood and Public which is why those platforms ship products so quickly," Gav Blaxburg, founder of Wolf Financial, a popular online trader enclave, said in a call. "Robinhood has built enough trust rebuilding its brand since Gamestop and they're allowing agents to trade literally everything."

events.title: Trump administration is examining whether a diesel export ban is feasible, Treasury secretary says
events.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the Trump administration is considering a full or partial ban on diesel exports. President Donald Trump said he supports an export ban. "I've said let's not send out the diesel. We make a lot of diesel," Trump said. The Trump administration is looking into whether implementing a diesel export ban would ease record high prices for the critical fuel, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Tuesday. "We're examining whether it's feasible in terms of the overall refining capacity and whether a full or partial ban would work," Bessent said at a bilateral meeting between President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the United Nations. Trump said Tuesday he's advocated for a diesel export ban during internal administration deliberations. The president said a decision would quickly be made "one way or another" on whether to implement a ban. "I've said let's not send out the diesel. We make a lot of diesel," Trump told reporters. Republican lawmakers including Sen. Chuck Grassley of Iowa have called for an export ban as high diesel prices hit farmers and truckers ahead of the November midterm elections. Diesel in the U.S. has surged to a record high $6.53 per gallon, almost $3 above the level last year, according to data from AAA. In California, diesel costs $8.44 per gallon. Fuel prices have jumped as the wars in Eastern Europe and the Middle East have slashed global refining capacity. Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries have forced Moscow to implement a diesel export ban. Refineries in the Middle East have also come under attack from Iran and its Houthi allies. And product exports through the Strait of Hormuz are constrained due to Iranian threats to tankers. The oil industry lobby group the American Petroleum Institute warned that "restricting U.S. energy exports would only compound the problem—exacerbating refining challenges and ultimately hurting consumers." "The answer is more supply and more flexibility—not new restrictions that risk making a difficult situation worse," API CEO Mike Sommers said in a statement. U.S. refiners have rushed to take advantage, ramping up diesel exports to help supply the world and reap sky-high profits. Diesel cost around $207 a barrel Tuesday, more than $100 above the price of crude oil. Diesel plays an essential role in the economy. It fuels the trucks and trains that deliver goods to market and the farm equipment that harvests crops. Higher diesel prices trickle down to consumers in higher grocery bills and what they pay for consumer products.

events.title: Climate finance needs an overhaul
events.summary: Tim’s view For developing countries, more green tech capital doesn’t always translate to a cheaper and cleaner energy system. There’s more money than ever available from private and public financial institutions for investments in clean tech in emerging economies: nearly $400 billion in 2025 , according to the Climate Policy Initiative, double the sum five years ago. It’s not enough — countries agreed at the COP summit in Azerbaijan to hit $1.3 trillion annually by 2035 — but I remember coming to Climate Week a few years ago and hearing a lot more anxiety about this subject than I’ve heard this year. One reason is that clean tech is so much cheaper that there’s more bang for the buck. Evidence is also piling up that these investments are much less risky than many investors feared: A recent study of lending from development banks to private enterprises in emerging economies since 1994 found an average default rate of 3.5% , similar to that in advanced economies. The bigger challenge isn’t just getting more capital, but making sure it actually leads to lower poverty and lower emissions. “There’s a lot of good intent,” Tariye Gbadegesin, CEO of Climate Investment Funds, a World Bank-backed pool of concessional capital for clean energy, told me. “But we need to be better at converting that into outcomes.” One lesson Gbadegesin has learned in her years in this field is that climate finance investments work best when they are coordinated with a country’s finance ministry, rather than energy or environmental officials, which has often been the status quo. Development banks shouldn’t just dump cash into individual clean tech projects, she said, but rather be proactive about helping developing countries fix their energy market regulations so they become more attractive to private investors, and so that the energy system as a whole, from generation to grids to end users, functions better. More financial innovation is also needed to mitigate the risk of losses introduced when imported hardware is paid for in US dollars, but energy is sold in local currency. “That’s really the fundamental challenge,” she said. Jonathan Berman, CEO of the Shell Foundation, who I interviewed at Semafor’s The Next 3 Billion event, added that more attention should focus on consumers’ budget constraints — that is, diverting more climate finance to the engineering and manufacturing improvements needed to drive the cost of clean tech down ever further. “People assume that if you use these billions of dollars and build these clean energy systems, that the demand will just come. That’s not true, and it’s less true now even than it was six months ago,” he said, as the fallout from the Iran war has weakened household budgets. Micro-lending and other financial products designed to make clean tech adoption more affordable to low-income households doesn’t work in a world where each new day feels less predictable than the last, he said, so “we probably should be driving towards no financing at all in as many of the use cases as possible.” Notable While development banks’ climate funding hit a record high last year , the World Bank has been pulling back on key goals.

events.title: Zelenskyy says Ukraine ready for ‘energy ceasefire,’ calls for trilateral meeting with Putin, Trump
events.summary: Zelenskyy said Ukraine is ready for an “energy ceasefire” with Russia, provided Moscow stops attacks on critical infrastructure. Ukraine's president also urged Trump to organize a trilateral meeting with Putin, saying the leaders should move “as quickly as possible” to end the war. Zelenskyy also called on Trump to engage Chinese President Xi Jinping, saying he has influence over Putin, as Kyiv braces for another winter of attacks on its energy infrastructure. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has called on U.S. President Donald Trump to organize a trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin , saying the world leaders need to move "as quickly as possible" to bring an end to the war. Zelenskyy spoke with Trump on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York on Tuesday. The high-stakes meeting provided Ukraine's president with a rare sit-down opportunity to discuss ways to bring an end to Russia's full-scale invasion , further U.S. air defense support and security guarantees for Kyiv. A winter package of Patriot missiles and licenses to produce the weapons domestically were two priorities for Ukraine over the coming months, Zelenskyy said. "President Trump, our teams, and I spoke about how to end the war. This is the priority. We are ready. I'm not sure Russia is ready as of today, but anyhow, we spoke about an energy ceasefire," Zelenskyy said overnight via social media, providing a roundup of his comments to reporters at the UNGA. Ukraine's president confirmed Kyiv is ready to agree to an energy truce on the condition that Russia does not attack its energy, electricity and heating infrastructure, as well as its water supplies. Trump has previously called on Ukraine to stop targeting Russian oil refineries with drone strikes, which he says are "hurting the world" as fuel supply disruptions from the Ukraine and Iran wars propel U.S. diesel prices to a record high . In a post Monday on Truth Social , the U.S. president said Russia had "unfortunately lost control" of its diesel oil industry due to the war. "I think the most important move President Trump can make – he can organize a trilateral meeting where the leaders can raise all the sensitive issues and try to end the war," Zelenskyy said. Asked whether his comments mean he's prepared to meet directly with Putin and Trump to bring an end to the war, Zelenskyy replied: "I'm ready. I said it, I'm ready anytime when all the sides will be ready. I think we all need to move as quickly as possible." CNBC has contacted a White House spokesperson and Russia's Embassy in London for comment and is awaiting a response. A meeting between Putin and Zelenskyy before expert-level discussions have taken place would be a waste of time, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Wednesday, according to Russia's state-run news agency RIA Novosti . "Regarding Putin's meeting with Zelensky, our position is well known. Putin said that Zelensky, if he wishes, can come to Moscow," Peskov said. Zelenskyy: Xi has 'influence on Putin' On his meeting with Zelenskyy, Trump told reporters that he had spoken with his Ukrainian counterpart about finding a solution to end Russia's war. He also referenced a diplomatic push to bring an end to the conflict during his speech to UNGA delegates. "We will get that one done," Trump said. Diplomatic talks have stalled as the U.S. has shifted focus to its war against Iran, although negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to Ukraine for the first time for talks with Zelenskyy earlier in the month. Ukraine, which has stepped up its strikes on Russian oil facilities and logistics infrastructure in recent months, also called on Trump to discuss ways to bring an end to the war with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Wednesday. "I said to the President, very openly, that we think if he also engages President Xi – he has influence on Putin. If we want to end this war, not just in messages, we all have to work 24/7 for this, for the people," Zelenskyy said. Ukraine has insisted that Russian energy sites are legitimate military targets as it continues to resist Russian forces that invaded the country in early 2022. Russia's Defense Ministry has said it is planning "massive strikes" on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, amplifying fears of another winter assault.

events.title: I’m a travel influencer who works every day while building my own business. Here are 4 ways I avoid burnout.
events.summary: The offers and details on this page may have updated or changed since the time of publication. See our article on Business Insider for current information. Rhiannon Wood, 26, started her journey as a solo-traveler and 'micro influencer' by first taking odd jobs around the world. Courtesy of Rhiannon Wood Rhiannon Wood, 26, is a travel influencer with about 60,000 Instagram followers. She works without an agent, preferring the freedom that comes with managing her own content. Here are the ways she avoids burnout from the extra workload an agent would normally absorb. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Rhiannon Wood , a 26-year-old travel micro influencer who runs a social media business and leads group tours around the world. It has been edited for length and clarity. I built my social media following from the ground up as a postgrad student working odd jobs around the world. Today, my work as a travel influencer continues to grow by the day, both in my following and in the number of brand deals I secure. I also partner with tourism companies to earn money leading adventure group trips around the world, though I'm building my own travel agency to launch next year. I take pride in doing everything myself, but there's a downside to taking on all the work: it sometimes feels like I'm skirting on the edge of burnout. I work almost every day negotiating deals, planning trips, scheduling posts, and engaging with my audience. While some influencers hire a social media agent to reduce their workload, I choose to work without one. Earlier this year, several agencies offered to take 25% to 30% of my earnings in exchange for potentially securing more brand deals — and income — for me. Ultimately, I declined. It's unclear whether working without an agent earns me more or less money, but, for now, I prefer the freedom and control of handling the work myself. I can post and interact with my followers exactly when and how I want. I also have a highly engaged account , which I've used to build trust with the online and offline communities I've cultivated over the years. One bad interaction could jeopardize that trust. Still, I've had to learn that working every day isn't sustainable. I've gotten better at stepping away from my work and making time to rest, rather than feeling like I always need to be doing something. Here's how I stay on top of my work while ensuring I have a life outside it. Learn how to say no to plans Rhiannon Wood is a social media influencer who leads travel group trips around the world. Courtesy of Rhiannon Wood I'm normally the sort of person who says yes to everything . But for the first time, I'm saying no to travel plans later this year and instead am choosing to stay in one place for longer. I think it's important to recognize that rest — as much as work, travel, and having fun — is a priority, too. I'm still learning how to say no to plans, or at least how to schedule in no plans at all. I scheduled a rest period for myself this summer because I signed up for a lot of group trips from late last year through the end of this September, and I am so glad I was able to rest for a week to reset my mind and body. Understand what rest looks like for you Rhiannon Wood emphasizes taking rest when needed and to not feel bad about doing so. Courtesy of Rhiannon Wood For me, rest involves stopping, sitting, and doing nothing for an entire day without feeling bad about it. I'm a big believer that taking the time to rest will eventually make you more productive. Working out can also be a form of rest for some, including me. Going to the gym and the climbing gym is a big hobby of mine, and I never film content or do work there. Instead, I see it as personal gain: I'm able to go at my own pace, on my own time. Adopt a positive frame of mind Rhiannon Wood has amassed over 60,000 followers on Instagram. Analytics aren't the only measure of success, she said, pointing also to the community she has made over the years. Courtesy of Rhiannon Wood If I keep telling myself I'm burned out from work, I'll believe it. The same goes for telling myself that I'm rested, have a lot of time to myself, and am excited about what's next: positive affirmations often lead me to positive results in my life and work. I take this mindset into how I look at my account's engagement analytics, too. While it is healthy to validate your emotions, feel them fully, and understand what is causing you stress, it's also healthy to find a silver lining in whatever is causing it. If I see a decrease in engagement or my follower count, I try to look at my work from an external frame of mind and be grateful for the number of spots for a group trip I've sold, for example, which means that the people who are going on them want to spend time with my community and me. That's arguably more important than my follower count, anyway. Have delusional self-belief in yourself Rhiannon Wood said she can count on her strong work ethic and positive mindset to carry her through the ups and downs of her career. Courtesy of Rhiannon Wood I try to remind myself that taking risks is necessary if I want to be rewarded in my line of work. Nothing comes easily, and most goals require you to chip away at them little by little. When work feels more stressful than usual, I focus on chipping away at my tasks in a sensible order. Even if I can't yet see exactly how my career path will unfold, I believe in myself and my ability to get where I want to go because I know I'm ambitious and have a strong work ethic. It's a sort of delusional self-belief, but it's served me well. I might not have enough money or all the answers right now, but I believe I'll find a way to make it happen. Somehow, it usually works out. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Nearly 10% of borrowers opted for riskier mortgages last week, as rates soared over 7%
events.summary: The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loans increased last week to 7.12% from 6.97% The ARM share of mortgage applications jumped to 9.8% Applications to refinance a home loan dropped 3% for the week and were 62% lower than the same week one year ago. Mortgage rates soared to the highest level since 2024 last week, causing loan demand to fall back again and more borrowers to opt for riskier loans. Total application volume decreased 1.5% from the previous week, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association's seasonally adjusted index. The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances, $832,750 or less, increased to 7.12% from 6.97%, with points rising to 0.73 from 0.72, including the origination fee, for loans with a 20% down payment. Applications to refinance a home loan dropped 3% for the week and were 62% lower than the same week one year ago. That was the lowest level since February 2025. The 30-year fixed loan was 78 basis points, or more than three-quarters of a percentage point lower, at the same time last year. Applications for a mortgage to purchase a home fell 1% for the week and were 11% lower year over year. The fall housing market, usually the second busiest compared with spring, is now underway, but real estate agents are already noting a sharp pullback due to higher rates. Buyers and current homeowners are also searching for savings anywhere they can find them, even in riskier, adjustable-rate loans. Get Property Play directly to your inbox CNBC's Property Play with Diana Olick covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, delivered weekly to your inbox. "With fixed rates much higher, more borrowers opted for ARMs, with the ARM share reaching 9.8%, as rates for 5/1 ARMs were more than a percentage point lower than those for fixed rate loans," said Mike Fratantoni, senior vice president and chief economist at the MBA. The ARM share of applications the week before last was just 8.4%. During the first years of the pandemic, when rates were hitting multiple record lows, the ARM share was barely 3%. ARMs can carry a fixed rate for up to 10 years but will adjust either higher or lower depending on where the market is when that term is up. Mortgage rates moved slightly lower to start this week, according to a separate survey from Mortgage News Daily, as the price of oil fell and bond yields moved lower as a result.

events.title: UEFA’s Ceferin says FIFA trust still broken after Infantino investment row
events.summary: UEFA president speaks for the first time since FIFA said it would review its decision-making, says trust still broken. UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin says trust in world football has not ⁠been restored following the collapse of FIFA’s controversial private investment plan. The remarks, made in a video address to the ⁠Portugal Football Summit on Wednesday, were Ceferin’s first public comments since FIFA president Gianni Infantino offered a review of the governing body’s decision-making. list 1 of 4 Afghan cyclist who escaped Taliban wins Asian Games silver medal list 2 of 4 The return of Palestinian football: ‘We are a people who must live’ list 3 of 4 La Liga President Tebas slams Real Madrid refereeing ‘conspiracy’ claims list 4 of 4 ‘Disgraceful’: Did India bully umpires to win Japan T20 cricket match? Ceferin said unity, transparency and governance that served the wider game were essential to maintaining trust in football. “Yet not everyone places the game above their own ambitions.” “Trust in our sport rests on three pillars: unity, transparency, and governance that serves the many, not the few. ‌In recent times, all three were disregarded by people who had sworn to protect them. “The project that shattered the unity of world football may be abolished, but the trust it broke has not returned, and repairing it is our work now.” Ceferin did not name Infantino or FIFA, but his comments were an apparent reference to the abandoned proposal to sell a 20 percent stake in FIFA’s commercial rights, including the World Cup, to private investors. The plan ⁠was dropped in July after fierce opposition from UEFA, the Asian Football ⁠Confederation and the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football (CONCACAF). “Football is not for sale,” Ceferin said. “That is the message UEFA has carried for years, and I’m certain this summit will carry it further.” His intervention came two days after Infantino sought to address the fallout in a letter ⁠to the FIFA Council and the presidents of all 211 member associations. He said he would ask the council whether it wanted to commission an ⁠independent external review of FIFA’s governance framework for major strategic initiatives ⁠and proposed consultations with confederations, member associations and other stakeholders on strengthening its decision-making processes. He said any review could examine the roles of the president, bureau, council and congress and ways to improve transparency and accountability. The letter has so far failed ‌to win over several federations that had criticised Infantino over the investment proposal. Infantino has said he remains fully committed to leading FIFA and is expected to seek another term at the presidential ‌election ‌in March 2027. Ceferin said those running the sport needed to remember whom they served. “The game will remain safe if those who govern it remember whom they govern it for,” he said.

events.title: I bought cardigans from Old Navy, Gap, and Banana Republic. They were all nice, but I'll be wearing one all season long.
events.summary: I ordered similar cardigans from Old Navy, Gap, and Banana Republic. Karen Santos for BI On crisp fall mornings when I don't have the energy to put together an outfit, I reach for my favorite cardigan. This versatile sweater is easy to style with a T-shirt and jeans for a casual day, or layer over a dress when I want something a little more polished. However, I wanted to find a new go-to cardigan I'd actually reach for on repeat, so I tested similar styles from three brands I already shop regularly — Old Navy, Gap, and Banana Republic . A good cardigan is a fall-fashion staple. Karen Santos for BI I bought one from each store, then wore them for a variety of occasions. I compared the cardigans based on comfort, material, design, fit, and quality. Although I loved them all, there's one I know I'll be wearing consistently this season. The option from Old Navy was the most classic. Karen Santos for BI I'm a fan of Old Navy for its range of wardrobe basics within a reasonable price range, so I knew I'd find a decent cardigan there. I ordered the SoSoft cotton crew-neck cardigan in a chocolate brown colorway, and was drawn to the rich, fall-ready hue and traditional knit design. Once I put it on, I loved these features even more. The material felt comfortable and soft on my skin. When I checked the tag, I was pleasantly surprised to see that it was crafted from 100% cotton. This cardigan cost me $43, which is slightly higher than Old Navy's usual pricing, but worth it for such a soft feel. Karen Santos for BI However, the fit made me feel a bit frumpy when it was buttoned up, and the fabric sagged a bit loosely around my waist and shoulders. So, I wore this sweater unbuttoned and layered over a tank for a night out to dinner and drinks with friends. I paired it with capris and kitten heels , which looked elevated and on-trend. Once the weather cools down more, this cardigan would be a stylish layering piece with a scarf or overcoat. Next, I tested the Gap cardigan, which offered a more relaxed and versatile look. Karen Santos for BI Gap is one of my tried-and-true retailers for clothing essentials , and its website offers a wide variety of cardigan styles to choose from. I went with the modern crewneck cardigan , also in a warm-brown shade. After taking it out of the package, I noticed that the material — made of 58% cotton, 38% modal, and 4% elastane — was more similar to that of a T-shirt than a sweater. I didn't mind it, though. I actually think it makes this option more versatile for casual, athleisure, and elevated ensembles. Karen Santos for BI I wore this one with a pair of baggy jeans to run errands, and it stayed comfortable and breathable throughout the day. However, I didn't think the material felt as durable as the knit cardigan from Old Navy. Plus, it cost $50, which seemed a bit steep for the more casual piece. Still, I thought it was a decent option. In my opinion, the Banana Republic cardigan was worth the money. Karen Santos for BI Banana Republic is Gap Inc.'s more luxurious brand, and I admire the store's elevated take on basic styles. I ordered the crinkle-knit cropped cardigan in an olive-green tone, and was immediately drawn to the neutral, fall-appropriate hue. I also loved the intricate ribbed-knit detailing. After putting it on, I got even more excited about this piece. The body-hugging, slightly cropped fit was flattering and modern. I paired it with dark-wash jeans, a belt, and boots for a work event , and I felt confident networking throughout the night. Karen Santos for BI However, I didn't think the material — made from 72% cotton and 28% nylon — was super breathable. It was thin but slightly rough on the skin, and I felt my underarms sweating after only a few hours. Despite this, I fell in love with the overall design of this cardigan. Although I normally wouldn't pay $120 for basics, I think the cost per wear I'll get from sporting this regularly justifies the investment. Overall, all the cardigans were nice, but the one from Banana Republic was my favorite. Business Insider reached out to Old Navy, Banana Republic, and Gap for comment. events.title: OpenAI is enlisting an influencer army to make it look 'good for the world'
events.summary: OpenAI; Getty Images; Alyssa Powell/BI OpenAI is ramping up its influencer strategy as AI hate spikes. It's asking creators to share how ChatGPT is improving their lives and is "good for the world." Not on the messaging agenda: killer robots or noisy data centers. AI's reputation is in hot water. Can influencers save it? OpenAI has been ramping up its creator marketing efforts as AI safety concerns take center stage. The company isn't asking influencers to assuage fears that a rogue AI could destroy humanity . Instead, it's prompting them to showcase why ChatGPT is "cool , " per one influencer talent manager , or how it can support work that's "good for the world," according to one campaign pitch viewed by Business Insider. OpenAI doubled the number of sponsored Instagram posts promoting ChatGPT from 61 in June to 122 in July, and then increased it further to 141 in August, according to data compiled by the influencer marketing platform HypeAuditor. Business Insider reviewed dozens of sponsored posts for OpenAI's ChatGPT product, and spoke with six managers and creators who had worked with the company. The company is casting a wide net, reaching out to parenting and fitness influencers as well as tech-savvy creators to broaden its user base and grow its advertising business. The message: ChatGPT can help you parent, run a business, create content, plan a workout, and be a good person. OpenAI's influencer strategy can be split into two buckets: getting businesses to pay for enterprise tools and keeping millions of consumers coming back to ChatGPT. Working with OpenAI can be risky for creators. Some influencers who post sponsored content for AI companies are getting dragged by their audiences. A small group of creators who attended an OpenAI brand trip in August were told their content was "morally bankrupt" and "dystopian" in their comments sections. That hasn't stopped companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Higgsfield AI from pitching influencers. "In the five inboxes that I manage alone, every single day, I would say at least 15 emails are from an AI company or some AI feature," Amanda Acevedo, a talent manager at G&B Digital Management, told Business Insider. Creator Natasha Badger, who makes content about marketing and tech, said it was a "big war" between AI companies over "who can get the most market share and work with the most influencers." Influencers are painting OpenAI's portrait Creators are a crucial part of OpenAI's public relations. They're "how people get information and learn about our products," an OpenAI spokesperson said. Founders-turned-influencers have been the cream of the crop for OpenAI's #ad strategy. Acevedo said the company is keen on working with creators who can tell a vivid story about how they're strategically using AI to "build an actual business." Badger, for instance, worked with OpenAI in July to promote its ChatGPT Work tools. She's one of many influencer-entrepreneurs the AI company is casting in short-form video ads across Instagram and TikTok. In the sponsored post, Badger walks through how she used ChatGPT to build a presentation. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Natasha Badger (@natashabadger) "Most people following any of us have ChatGPT already," Badger said. "They don't need to convert users. It's more getting people to continue going to ChatGPT as your go-to LLM." OpenAI has been open to hearing influencers' content ideas rather than pushing a narrow script, insiders who've worked on campaigns said. "They want it to be catered to a specific use case that resonates with our lives and day-to-day," Badger said. OpenAI's influencer strategy, however, is growing well beyond B2B marketing. At the start of September, The Shade Room — a meme page with over 28 million Instagram followers — shared a sponsored post with ChatGPT. It wasn't a demo of how AI could streamline your workflow. It was a word search puzzle generated by ChatGPT. One talent manager said OpenAI representatives had expressed interest in working with fitness creators, since health and running questions are such common use cases for ChatGPT. HypeAuditor's analysis of hundreds of Instagram posts promoting ChatGPT found these were the core topics: Coding Productivity Career development Health Travel Education Content creation Shopping Home projects In a recent back-to-school partnership, Martha Dove, a mother of five, shared how she's using ChatGPT to help her kids with their math homework. The ad specifically promotes tools like ChatGPT's "study mode" and teen safety features. Acevedo said there's one key message AI brands across the board are pushing with creators: AI is an assistant, "not a replacement." "I'm still her mom and her teachers are still her teachers — this isn't replacing any of that," Dove emphasized in her video. OpenAI is beefing up its influencer resources As OpenAI hires more influencers, it's building a team of tech veterans who know the inner workings of creator partnerships. OpenAI has hired a handful of talent from platforms like Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, and Snapchat, according to a review of OpenAI staffers' LinkedIn profiles. Most visibly, in February, OpenAI poached Charles Porch, Instagram's longtime head of partnerships. Charles Porch joined OpenAI after leaving Meta in 2026. Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images for Vanity Fair The AI company has also tapped the influencer marketing agency Viral Nation — which has worked with major tech companies like Meta, Google, and Uber — to handle elements of its creator campaigns. One job of these longtime influencer marketers is to make creators feel like AI isn't the enemy. "There is so much tension between AI and the creator economy," Acevedo said. She sees commissioning sponsored posts as a way for OpenAI to "help bridge that gap — that we're not against each other." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Muse's normie-friendly design is the playbook for how Meta can win at AI
events.summary: Meta's Muse AI agent mascot Meta Muse, Meta's AI agent , has become a hit app. Meta knows how to design normie-friendly apps — and that matters, a lot. As Zuck would say, it passes his "mother" test. Ultimately, Meta's edge in the AI battle is its vast edge in creating and cross-promoting consumer apps. With Meta's Muse agent shooting to the top of the App Store charts , I'm reminded of something Mark Zuckerberg said earlier this year. "There's a lot of agents out there," Mark Zuckerberg told investors on an April earnings call. "There aren't that many that I would want to give to my mother." The Meta CEO said the company was willing to tinker until it had an AI agent "more polished and dialed and easy" than the competition. Something that "just works." Something that would pass his "mother" test . Nearly a half a year later, that strategy is paying off, with Meta's Muse agent overtaking ChatGPT as the top free AI app. This is the playbook for how Meta wins at AI — not by having the best frontier models, but by having the most successful consumer app and pushing it out to its billions of existing users. People seem to like Muse! Like, really like it! I've been playing around with it myself , and am pleasantly delighted by some of the tasks I've asked it to do (to be fair, it's also failed a bunch of tasks I asked it to do). It's debatable whether Muse is the most powerful or "best" agent. Instinct is a similar product that I know one of my colleagues was really enjoying, and it seems to have a growing fanbase. Others have noticed how similar Muse is to OpenClaw , which appeals to more technically proficient users and kicked off the personal AI agent craze. we built muse from scratch, but it is definitely heavily inspired as a product by openclaw. After I used openclaw in january I bought hundreds of mac minis for the MSL team and lots of us fell in love with using openclaw (and other personal agents). @steipete is a genius and his… — Nat Friedman (@natfriedman) September 21, 2026 But neither Instinct nor OpenClaw has the sheer power of Meta's massive user base, where it can cross-promote its apps. Nor do they have Meta's knack for creating a normie-friendly, easy-to-use consumer app. That last part is the key. Say what you want about Meta, but you have to concede they are very good at making apps so easy to use and popular that your mother (or even grandmother) can — and loves — to use. They make apps that are so easy and compelling to use that their biggest criticism is that their apps are addictive and people — kids, even! — spend too much time using them. Meta hasn't been winning the AI race in terms of creating the most cutting-edge models , so far. Up until now, they've failed at creating the most popular consumer-facing AI apps. They launched celebrity-voiced chatbots early on (a John Cena one now lives in infamy because it was found to engage in lewd talk with what it was told was an underage user), as well as the ability to create your own character chat on Instagram. Their AI video app, Vibes , was a huge flop compared to OpenAI's Sora 2 at launch. But finally, Muse is the thing that clicked. It's impressive enough it's won over the tech crowd, but easy enough to use that regular people are playing around with it. The biggest hurdle of an AI agent for normies is figuring out what kinds of things you can ask it to do — and nudging people in the right direction for how to start using a product is something Meta is great at. It didn't need to be the most bleeding-edge AI; it didn't even need to be the first AI agent app. It just needs to be the easiest to use that gets the job (mostly) done. As one former Googler summed it up : "User experience matters. Design matters. Making products easy to use matters." Here's Meta's play right now: Let Anthropic and OpenAI be the ones to worry about AI accidentally killing humanity and all the burdens, regulations, and misery that go along with that. There's little upside in rolling in the muck with the doomers or the accelerationists. Instead, Meta will capture the normies who just want something to help manage their inbox — and all the spoils that come with that. It's not hard to imagine how Muse could become lucrative for Meta — a company that mainly runs an ad business — as a shopping app. Amazon has already blocked it , but other services like PayPal and Shopify are partnering with Muse, happy to let Muse connect shoppers through their payments. Meta has the money and political capital to get massive data centers built. They have the ability to aggressively promote their internal apps, like Threads, to their billions of users. It's the game plan Zuckerberg described to Wall Street back in April, while bemoaning how complicated the AI agent OpenClaw was to install and set up. "I think if you had something like that, that worked quite a bit better than those systems and was easy enough that people could just get, then I think you go from having something that hundreds of thousands or millions of people are going to use to something that is going to be addressable to billions of people." And eventually, when you win billions of users, you win the war. Read the original article on Business Insider

Science, not chaos, ensued January 26, 2026 UK utility provider Southern Water is turning fiber-optic telecoms cables into underground sensors in an effort to find leaks in its water network. The privatized biz is trialing tech from Lightsonic that uses Openreach's fiber network to detect leaking pipes. Openreach - BT's infrastructure arm - and Affinity Water, which supplies parts of southern England, tested the system in March. As The Register reported at the time , the system analyzes tiny changes in light traveling through fiber-optic cables to detect vibrations caused by nearby underground leaks. Machine learning helps distinguish those signals from traffic, roadworks and other background noise, and estimates where the water is escaping. Lightsonic says the resulting location data allows engineers to investigate and repair leaks more quickly. It claims the tech is already preventing the loss of more than four million liters (about a million gallons) of water per day across 650 km (400 miles) of the UK's water network. Southern Water is adopting the technology after one of Britain's hottest and driest summers on record, with almost three-quarters of England officially under drought conditions. Southern England is among the country's most water-stressed regions. The utility said Lightsonic's work with Affinity Water and Openreach influenced its decision to run the trial. Southern Water hopes the trial will help it meet Ofwat's leakage-reduction targets for 2030 and strengthen its drought resilience by easing pressure on reservoirs and water abstraction. The company provides water and wastewater services across parts of Hampshire, the Isle of Wight, West Sussex, East Sussex, and Kent. "We've reduced leakage across our network for three consecutive years and continue to invest in innovative techniques and technologies to find and fix leaks even more effectively," said Wayne Novelli, Southern Water's leakage and network strategy manager. "We've been impressed by the leakage reduction metrics and proven success of Lightsonic's technology and are looking forward to working with the team to trial a new way of detecting and tackling them." Southern Water's efforts to conserve clean water come against a less flattering record on wastewater. A court this week fined it £2.4 million ($3.1 million) over several pollution incidents in Kent. That followed a £7.1 million ($9.4 million) fine in July for illegal sewage discharges that forced beaches in Thanet to close.
