events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts ACT chief minister points finger at US president over Canberra fuel costs but opposition unconvinced US President Donald Trump is being blamed for Canberra's high fuel prices. ( ABC News/Supplied: AP: Evan Vucci ) Canberra is the most expensive capital city in the country for motorists to fill up their tanks. ACT Chief Minister Andrew Barr says anger over the costs should be directed at the US president, but the ACT opposition says there are problems closer to home. The ACT Legislative Assembly will hold an inquiry into the capital's high fuel prices. The ACT's chief minister says Canberrans should be "rightly angry" about high fuel prices in the territory but says that anger should first be aimed at United States President Donald Trump. Canberra is currently the most expensive capital city in the country for both petrol and diesel. The ACT Legislative Assembly has now supported a move to hold an inquiry into the capital's high fuel prices, with a particular focus on examining why ACT motorists pay more for fuel than people just over the border in New South Wales. Oil prices have dropped but Australian motorists should remain wary The global benchmark for oil prices has fallen by more than $2 a barrel, but what does this mean for Australians at the bowser? Chief Minister Andrew Barr said there were several factors that resulted in the ACT's high fuel prices, including transport costs to get fuel from Sydney, a lack of retail competition and less fuel being sold due to a rise in hybrid and electric vehicles. "Cars and trucks are more fuel efficient now than they were 25 years ago," Mr Barr said. "All of the fixed infrastructure costs associated with a petrol and diesel distribution network are now being spread across fewer litres of sale." However, Mr Barr said "international factors" were clearly to blame for the current cost increases for fuel. 'Canberra tax' is culprit: opposition Opposition leader Mark Parton, who initiated the call for the fuel price inquiry, said Mr Barr was "deflecting" by talking about the US President. "Donald Trump has got nothing to do with that; he hasn't given some blessing to Queanbeyan, Jerrabomberra, Goulburn and Braidwood." Canberra Liberals leader Mark Parton has accused the ACT chief minister of "deflecting" when it comes to Canberra's high fuel costs. ( ABC News: Luke Stephenson ) Mr Parton said he also "didn't buy" the argument around less fuel being sold in the ACT leading to high prices, instead blaming the "high cost of doing business" in the territory. "It's not fair for regular people in Canberra that they have to pay this 'Canberra tax' whenever they go to the petrol bowser." Calls for portable rental-bond scheme ACT Greens housing spokesperson Rebecca Vassarotti wants a portable rental-bond scheme. ( ABC News: Luke Stephenson ) Cost-of-living relief dominated debate in the Legislative Assembly on Wednesday, with the ACT Greens moving a motion to call on the ACT government to set up a portable rental-bond scheme . ACT Greens housing spokesperson Rebecca Vassarotti said the scheme would mean Canberra renters moving house would no longer have to find thousands of dollars while waiting for a previous bond to be returned. "What we are really focused on is providing a mechanism to take a little bit of pressure off renters and ensuring that they are not having to front up extra thousands of dollars if they don't need to." ACT Attorney-General Tara Cheyne says portable rental-bond schemes are costly. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) The assembly supported a watered-down Greens motion, allowing the government to investigate whether a portable rental-bond scheme, or another option, was the best way of reducing the financial burden on renters ACT Attorney-General Tara Cheyne said the government accepted it was a "real problem". "We shouldn't decide the architecture of a scheme before understanding who it will help, who it may exclude, what risks it creates and what it will cost.

events.title: Five Signals From The 2026 Functional Verification Study
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Functional verification is no longer only about closing the design. It is increasingly about understanding the system before silicon becomes the first place where all interactions are fully revealed. The forthcoming 2026 Siemens EDA and Wilson Research Group Functional Verification Study indicates that the IC verification problem is changing in nature, not simply growing in complexity. Declining first-silicon success, increased CPU/GPU/AI accelerator-class participation, near-universal reported embedded processor content across implementation categories, a broadening verification ecosystem, and greater visibility of firmware-, safety-, and security-related respin contributors all point toward a shift from verifying designs to building system confidence in software-driven silicon systems. events.title: Multi-Agent AI Systems Must Work Like An Orchestra Without A Conductor
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Multi-agentic systems have evolved into a dynamic, task-based organization of skills with a flatter hierarchy than a traditional military force, and some are headless. Agentic capabilities will also come from physical, deterministic engines, and those agents will talk to other agents in different formats to help ensure 100% accuracy, which AI models alone cannot achieve. Human effort is needed to ensure a design can be copyrightable, and on-prem proprietary models are another way to ensure prompt IQ and IP are not lost. Experts At The Table : Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss recent developments and challenges when using agentic AI for chip design, with Matt Graham, senior group director of verification software product management at Cadence ; Harrison Balistreri, head of business development and strategic partnerships at ChipAgents ; Alexander Petr, senior director and portfolio manager at Keysight EDA ; Sathish Balasubramanian, head of product for EDA AI at Siemens EDA ; and Anand Thiruvengadam, executive director and head of AI product management at Synopsys . This roundtable was held behind closed doors at the recent Design Automation Conference. What follows are excerpts of that discussion. This is the third part of a three-part series. Part one is here . Part two is here . L-R: Synopsys’ Thiruvengadam; Keysight’s Petr; Cadence’s Graham; ChipAgents’ Balistreri; and Siemens’ Balasubramanian. SE: Many agentic flows involve a mixture of experts (MoE) or a hierarchy of multi-agents with some type of leader at the top. What developments are you seeing there? Is it a top-down, military-style organization with various security and access clearances, or more of a horizontal team? Graham: It is becoming much flatter than an army. If you’d asked me a year ago, I might have said, yes, it is a big hierarchy of agents. There will be mini agents, sub agents, and low agents. There will be generals and lieutenants and whatever else, all the way up. But AI in general, not just EDA, we are migrating much more toward a flat set of skills, or capabilities, or features, or knowledge, or whatever the word is you want to use to describe it. Everything is overloaded with terms. What we’re seeing becomes a much more dynamic, task-based organization of skills into almost dynamic agents. There is one general, if you like, or commander. Balasubramanian: Orchestrator. Graham: Right. And everything else below tends to be much flatter. I can pick and choose quickly to assemble my troops, but it’s much less like an army with a mechanized division and an airborne division, or something else. We have troops. Those troops have skills, and we assemble the right troops for the task dynamically, because we’re not bound, as armies are, by logistical and physical reality. Petr: You’re better off comparing it to an orchestra. You have one conductor, and you have groups who play certain instruments. They can play individually, or they can play together. They can also play synchronously or asynchronously to achieve certain tunes and then play together. Balasubramanian: That’s very important. Even if it’s flat, the key thing is that everyone knows their part, and they also know how they connect to everyone else. Everyone knows the end goal. Nothing is siloed. They all play by the same tune. If you look at a symphony orchestra, everyone knows everyone else. They can read the notes. They know what to do, what not to do, how to do it. Petr: There are borders, guardrails. They all ground it. Balasubramanian: The term I see quite a bit is headless agents. There’s no concept of having a big master agent doing everything else. We call it a headless way of working, and it’s been quite popular on the software side. It’s coming here, and what I see going forward is customers are interacting with tools. They won’t even know what the tool is. From our side, we are going to build agentic capabilities coming out of the physical engines, or deterministic engines around those engines, and that’s going to be an agent on its own. It can talk to other agents. It can understand different formats and where it sits. It can talk to understand design. Designers can interact with it, make it do work. That’s where the future is going. Thiruvengadam: What Matt said is very interesting. We are essentially making the point that you should be thinking about digital organization—human organization, human hierarchy, digital hierarchy, roughly speaking —which is correct. But also, the fluidity of that is very important. It won’t be a rigid, hard structure. Ebb and flow will happen. It can change, depending on the complexity of the commands. The fluidity is very important. You will have a layer that orchestrates and calls upon ‘resources’ as needed to execute. This is very important. At some point in the future, it might graduate to something where it’s maybe autonomous. That is about abstraction again. We are talking about taking layer after layer of abstraction away, one by one, but we’re not there yet. Balistreri: We have products where agents propose hypotheses and do tournament-style ranking. We have a judging agent, but there’s a lot of nuance in this idea of agents, where you could throw many agents at the problem. But if they all come up with similar hypotheses for the problem, it doesn’t matter how many agents you deploy or how good your judging agent is. It has a lot to do with how you manage context, and it comes back to local versus global context. It doesn’t matter how you deploy agents if they all have the same local context. To get the benefit of deploying agents at scale, you need to manage which hypotheses each agent generates and where that context comes from. To do that, you also can’t have point agents. You can’t do point acceleration around one tool. Agents become powerful when they can deliver the full flow. The full flow requires encoding in your agent loops how to view some of this context and how to manage that, so that you get the benefit of many parallel agents instead of them just trying to converge on the same thing. Graham: There are two sides to that, and I agree for the most part. But I’ll draw a parallel to how synthesis changed electronic design. The vast majority of gates built now are synthesized gates. The agent writes RTL. Then, RTL gets synthesized. But there is still a certain percentage, depending on the application, that must be either hand-synthesized or laid out by hand. There will still be significant opportunity to accelerate the tools. I wouldn’t call it a point agent necessarily. But in agentifying the tool for a specific task, a smaller percentage will still need to be hand-coded, in the same way that we still hand-assemble some instructions for a PC or for any compute platform. events.title: Building A Connected, Contextual Data Backbone For AI-Driven Semiconductor Design
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Why design teams must organize before they optimize and how to utilize a purpose-built foundation for AI-ready data management across the chip design lifecycle. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is redefining what’s possible in semiconductor design. From intelligent layout generation to predictive verification and generative IP reuse, AI promises to transform Electronic Design Automation (EDA) workflows and accelerate innovation. Yet despite the growing potential, most design environments are not ready to harness AI effectively. The obstacle isn’t a lack of models or computational power—it’s the data. AI-enhanced EDA workflows depend on structured, contextualized, and verifiable data. Without it, AI cannot learn efficiently, scale effectively, or deliver trustworthy insights. Fragmented repositories, inconsistent metadata, and undocumented IP reuse all obscure the relationships that give design data meaning. When data lacks organization and traceability, AI-driven automation becomes unreliable and difficult to implement. The path to AI-driven design innovation begins with data organization, not algorithm selection. Before optimizing processes, semiconductor teams must first establish a strong, structured data foundation that connects every stage of the design lifecycle. This white paper explores why organizing data is the first and most critical step toward AI readiness—and how Keysight SOS provides the purpose-built infrastructure to achieve it. As AI SoCs integrate increasingly complex combinations of processors, accelerators, memory subsystems, and high-speed interfaces, verification challenges extend well beyond functional correctness. Modern designs must validate system integration, software interactions, interoperability, and performance across highly configurable third-party IP environments. This white paper explores how simulation-based verification helps engineering teams identify integration issues early and accelerate development cycles. The paper examines the evolving role of Verification IP (VIP), Test Groups, and SoC Verification Kits (SVKs) in modern semiconductor verification flows. Readers will learn how these solutions provide protocol expertise, reusable verification content, and pre-integrated test environments that reduce integration risk, improve verification efficiency, and enable consistent validation from early RTL development through system-level verification. How Verification IP (VIP) helps validate integration correctness, software interactions, interoperability, and system-level KPIs for complex interface-based designs. Why Test Groups provide a more scalable, use case-driven approach to interface verification than traditional monolithic test suites. events.title: Blog Review: Sept. 23
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Digital twins and thermal sensors; agentic AI workflows; physical AI needs new silicon; RF design changes. Siemens’ Matteo Depaola and Robin Bornoff examine how physics-based digital twins for electronics can enable a handful of carefully placed physical thermal sensors to provide the measurements needed to support many more virtual sensors throughout the system. Synopsys’ Thomas Andersen explores how agentic AI systems change the unit of work from an individual prompt, command, or recommendation to a goal-directed workflow. Cadence’s Max Zarco argues that traditional edge silicon can’t keep up with the demands of physical AI , which require multimodal workloads, stricter real-time constraints, and security anchored in hardware. Keysight’s Richard Duvall finds that AI is fundamentally changing RF design by using advanced statistical models, deep learning networks, and automated reasoning to explore vast, high-dimensional RF design spaces rapidly. Arm’s Julie Gaskin shares how neural workload profiling can help developers identify latency, expensive graph operations, and shader fallbacks in applications that use the ML extensions for Vulkan. The ESD Alliance’s Julie Rogers and Paul Cohen chat with Jay Vleeschhouwer of Griffin Securities about whether EDA growth is sustainable, the impact of AI, 2027 revenue predictions. Plus, check out the blogs featured in the latest Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials newsletter : Mitsubishi Chemical Group’s Hideaki Okamoto looks at why expanding computational capabilities and deeper co-development are changing how materials are moving from lab to fab. Amkor’s Chiung Lee outlines how thinner dies, taller stacks, and hybrid bonding are carrying NAND into the AI era , driven by data growth across consumer electronics, automotive, enterprise, and cloud. Lam Research’s Swapnil Kailash More illustrates how small imbalances between stacked nanosheets can distort device behavior in ways that are difficult to predict from geometry alone. Intel Foundry’s Lalitha Immaneni contends that design space exploration must become a core capability for advanced packaging and chiplet-based systems. Synopsys’ Larry Melvin discusses wafer-validated optical simulation for high-NA EUV applications, enabled by early lithography pathfinding, process optimization, and analysis. events.title: 'We've done nothing wrong': Firearms shop's gun laws plea after $800k loss
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Firearms businesses say they are struggling under Minns government's post-Bondi gun laws Topic: State and Territory Government Ms Malloy (right) says her parents' business has become worthless since the changes. ( ABC News: Alex Lewis ) Local firearms businesses claim they have lost hundreds of thousands of dollars in trade since the NSW government's post-Bondi gun laws passed in December. The Bondi terror attack, in which 15 people were killed, prompted the NSW parliament to pass Australia's strictest gun laws. The NSW Liberal Party has pledged to remove the caps and freeze the buyback. Firearms dealers have tearfully described losing retirement nest eggs and being forced to sell their home, blaming the Minns government's post-Bondi gun laws. Taylah Malloy and her mother Sarah Turner were among families who rallied at parliament on Wednesday, as six crossbenchers work to block Labor's buyback regulations and repeal new limits on ownership. Ms Turner says the business they have "nothing to retire on". ( Supplied ) Ms Malloy said her parents' business, Arms & Ammo, in the Newcastle suburb of Beresfield, was meant to fund their retirement but had become worthless since the changes. The massacre of 15 people at a Jewish celebration in December prompted the NSW parliament to pass Australia's strictest gun laws. Most licence holders were banned from owning more than four firearms and certain types now require stricter licences. Buyback offer 'a drop in the ocean' As part of the state's buyback scheme due to begin in November, dealers have been offered grants of up to $25,000. Ms Malloy said her parents' business had lost more than $800,000 in firearms trade alone, and described $25,000 as a "drop in the ocean". "There are people that are losing that amount per day within their businesses," she said. Ms Turner said her business had stock it could no longer sell because of the lower caps on ownership. "It's like being in quicksand," Ms Turner said. Ms Malloy's parents have a business based at Beresfield in Newcastle. ( Supplied ) The dealership could not recoup the costs of the firearms through the buyback scheme, she said, as it applies only to individual licence holders. Ms Turner broke down as she described how the family and clay target shooters and hunters had lost everything they built. Zac and Courtney Kirwan said they were preparing to shut their firearms, hunting and outdoors store at Castle Hill in Sydney's north-west after trade plunged 80 per cent. "It's just like turning off a tap," Mr Kirwan said. Part of Mr Kirwan's store in north-west Sydney. ( Supplied: Zac Kirwan ) He said the business, Badlands, supported the couple and their two young daughters, and employed five people. Now the family has had to sell a house and move back in with their parents. "We're basically losing everything. We have to find new jobs," Mr Kirwan said. "I think sometimes people don't realise, well the government doesn't realise how much damage they can do to personal lives with the stroke of a pen," he said. Mr Kirwan is expecting to close the firearms, hunting and outdoors store he runs with his wife in Sydney's north-west. ( ABC News: Alex Lewis ) Mr Kirwan described the $25,000 grant proposed as a "spit in the face", saying their business was "probably over $1 million down". "It's literally crushed us, and we've done nothing wrong." The premier's office has been approached for comment. In question time, Attorney General Michael Daley said it was "inarguable" there were "too many guns in our society". Upon announcing the buyback scheme in August, NSW Premier Chris Minns said: "This is a big undertaking, but the principle behind it is simple: fewer dangerous guns in our community means a safer New South Wales." Mr Daley says there are "too many guns in our society". ( ABC News: Nick Dole ) Disallowance motions to freeze buyback regulations While the state Liberals supported the reforms passed on Christmas Eve, the party has pledged to remove the caps and freeze the buyback. Last week, the opposition backed an attempt by independent Barwon MP Roy Butler to stop the buyback regulations by voting in favour of a disallowance motion. Another disallowance motion is set to be moved by the Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party (SFF) next month in the upper house, where the numbers are much tighter. The NSW Liberals have pledged to remove the caps and freeze the buyback. ( ABC News: Berge Breiland ) SFF MLC Mark Banasiak said stopping the regulations could come to a single vote. "I'm never confident, but I'm working my backside off to make sure we get this done," Mr Banasiak said.

events.title: Trump's energy adviser says Gulf must build new oil routes to bypass Strait of Hormuz
events.summary: Almost seven months into a war that has redrawn the global energy map, the man overseeing US President Donald Trump 's energy agenda says the fight over Middle East oil is no longer only about supply – it's about the routes that carry it. “We need to de-emphasise the strait [Hormuz],” says the head of America’s Energy Dominance Council, Jarrod Agen. “When Europe had to get off Russian gas, we looked at different corridors to get US LNG into Europe to replace the Russian gas. We want to do a similar system in the Gulf.” Speaking to On The Record with Hadley Gamble at the UN General Assembly , Mr Agen said the goal was redundancy: routes that cannot all be knocked out at once. That means “several routes, different corridors, either east-west, either bypassing the strait or getting up Turkey or into the Mediterranean”, he said, with the UAE and Saudi Arabia working as key partners with the US. “How do we make alternative routes beyond the bypass route so that no one route can be attacked and shut down the progress?” Mr Agen said. “The only person that can quarterback that is President Trump. He's the one that can get everybody around the table and get everyone to agree.” Since the Iran war erupted in February, Brent crude has swung from about $72 a barrel to a peak near $120, dipped below $70 by midsummer, and by mid-September was trading back above $104 as renewed attacks on shipping and energy infrastructure reversed earlier gains. Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz – the corridor that once carried more than 20 per cent of the world's oil trade – has collapsed by about 95 per cent, from more than 100 vessels a day to as few as five. War-risk insurance for tankers attempting the transit has surged into the millions of dollars a voyage. American motorists, meanwhile, have watched pump prices climb to their highest levels since 2023. Asked to set the scene, Mr Agen did not start with barrels – he started with bottlenecks. “The most important one globally is refining,” he said. “ Refining capacity here in the United States is at 100 per cent. We are tapped out.” He noted the imbalance across the globe. “Russia is down 30 per cent to 40 per cent refining. China has still some room to do more refining, more export,” he added. But the deeper shift, Mr Agen said, was strategic rather than technical, with the Middle East energy map permanently redrawn. “If you don't have your own energy supply that you can rely on, then it affects everything. It's not just your economy, it's your national security. And it's your whole foreign policy as well,” Mr Agen said. Pressed on cost, Mr Agen did not dispute that the numbers are large. “I mean, yes, the infrastructure commitment is going to be in the billions,” he said. “But look at the long-term benefits of it.” Asked to put a number to this new energy security premium, Mr Agen reframed what producers are buying. “It's almost incalculable, because energy security is national security,” he said. That calculus lands on top of an industry-wide investment gap that predates the war. Analysts at the International Energy Forum and S&P Global have put the annual upstream spending required until 2030 at between $400 billion and $640 billion. The figure is up sharply from the $483 billion peak reached in 2019, just to offset accelerating decline rates in existing fields – before a single dollar goes towards new bypass pipelines, storage or alternative Gulf export corridors . Mr Agen's framing suggests the war has added a security premium on top of that baseline: infrastructure spending Gulf states will now shoulder not to grow supply, but to insure it against the next disruption. Venezuela centre of the ‘energy universe’ Mr Agen was most emphatic when describing what he called the administration's core strategic bet: that the Western Hemisphere, not the Gulf, should anchor global energy security. “The President has made the Western Hemisphere the centre of the energy universe,” he said. “It is not in the Middle East. It is not in the East. It's the Western Hemisphere, Alaska, all the way down to Argentina. We are unleashing American energy. We are unleashing Venezuelan energy.” He said a new arrangement with Caracas was the clearest evidence. “This amazing deal that the President struck with Venezuela, where we're now opening 17 more prime fields – the US is now in partnership with Venezuela on this,” Mr Agen said. “This is the biggest oil deal in the history of the US. That sends a message to the world.” Asked whether that diminishes Opec’s relevance, he said: “What it means is we've become more important.” No sympathy for a slower transition On Europe's energy politics, Mr Agen credited a recent G20 energy ministerial meeting in Houston with a tonal shift away from climate targets and towards reliability. “There wasn't a lot of talk about net zero ,” he said. “It was more about energy security; affordability, reliable energy.” He singled out Poland and Italy for investing in LNG import and storage capacity, but dismissed the broader premise of a shift away from fossil fuels entirely. “This whole talk of energy transition – that's nonsense. It's energy addition,” he said. “Natural gas is secure. Nuclear is going to be secure. These are the things they should be investing in, not windmills and solar projects.” Relief for refiners Asked directly about prices at the pump, Mt Agen turned to domestic policy, contrasting the administration's approach with predecessors he accused of constraining supply. “In the past, California, Gavin Newsom, Joe Biden – they have all been trying to shut down refineries in the US , and this is what happens when you try to shut down refineries,” he said. “We're doing the opposite. We're bringing them in. We're asking them what they need.” He said the administration was examining use of the Defence Production Act to fast-track refinery funding. “This is weeks and months of getting more refining capacity online” – paired, he said, with regulatory relief modelled on rolling back California-style restrictions. “If we get more refined products on the market, that will drive down prices.” Whether that timeline holds may determine how much of the “security premium” American consumers ultimately absorb – and how long Gulf capitals are willing to bankroll a rerouted energy map before the war that made it necessary comes to an end.

events.title: In the age of AI, teaching networking principles remains more important than learning protocols
events.summary: A few weeks ago I took part in the SIGCOMM 2026 Education Workshop, provocatively titled “Networking Education in the Age of AI”. Perhaps that title isn’t provocative to most educators today, but it is to me: I’ve repeatedly voiced my skepticism about AI in education (and other fields). I was also a student in another “age of AI” in the mid-1980s, which was followed by one of several “AI Winters,” but of course that couldn’t happen again, right? Fortunately there was much more to the workshop than its title might suggest, and Larry and I came away with some fresh energy and new ideas on what we still need to do for our 7th edition. I should mention that the event was a successful hybrid event, thanks to some serious effort by the organizers and support from SIGCOMM to use professional camera operators and audio gear. There was no escaping the early wakeup call to attend an event eight time zones away, but at least I didn’t need to fly anywhere. The large number of remote participants and high-quality setup ensured that the interactions never devolved into local-only discussions (although I missed the coffee breaks). I’m going to have to leave out a lot of what was good about the workshop (especially since I only joined at lunchtime) but I recommend taking a look at the accepted papers and artifacts to get a sense of the level of creativity and enthusiasm that was brought to the occasion. Notably, the papers were not actually presented; in some cases they were summarized or provided a jumping off point for a discussion. But this was a real working session, not a set of paper presentations. Engaging students with design One highlight for me was co-chairing an open mic session with Jim Kurose. Jim’s networking book (co-authored with Ken Ross) is the leader in our field, with Computer Networks: A Systems Approach at best a distant second. In a discussion about different teaching approaches including the use of labs as a primary teaching tool, I asked a question about the role of programming assignments in driving adoption of a textbook, and Jim’s answer was something like “programming exercises, Wireshark labs, etc.—all important, but don’t underestimate the value of nice, animated PowerPoint slides.” It’s a reminder that we have more work to do than just writing a book if we want it to be chosen for classroom instruction. One reason this is challenging is that neither of us has taught using our book for a long time – in my case, all my classroom teaching was in graduate classes that used systems papers rather than a textbook as the assigned reading. There were a dozen speakers in the open mic session, all of whom had something worthwhile to say, but I’ll highlight a few things that stuck with me. Karen Sollins shared some experiences in modeling her systems classes on law school case studies. The idea is that the professor doesn’t deliver a lecture but rather assigns papers that get students to talk about what goes on in systems papers. They might discuss questions such as “what constraints led to this system design” or “what alternatives were considered by the designers.” This contrasts with the more traditional approach (which I recall using when I was teaching) of walking the students through the design as I understood it, hoping they would walk away with some insights. This importance of getting students to engage with the challenges of the design process came up over and over, and it gets to the heart of what we are trying to emphasize in our new book. To take an example, we don’t simply want students to read our book to learn how TCP works; we want them to understand the tradeoffs that have been made and broad challenges that any reliable transport has to deal with, such as the difficulty of accurate round-trip time estimation and of achieving stability in a control system with imperfect knowledge of current conditions. One approach to getting students engaged in design has them tackle problems in class without the use of computers, described as “Networking Unplugged”. For example, pairs of students are given a piece of rope and asked to design a mechanism to send bits along it, leading them to “discover” encoding techniques such as NRZ and various forms of modulation. Of course there was plenty of discussion about using AI in teaching. One positive view is that students could be given bigger and more realistic system-building and measurement assignments because of the availability of AI coding agents to take on the implementation tasks. One paper made this case and combined it with suggestions on how to assess how well students are learning by getting them to discuss the design. Test the learning, not the implementation. I remain skeptical of the value of using LLM-generated code in production, because of the risks of hard-to-detect bugs and difficulty of maintenance (among other concerns), and my experience suggests code generation is a small part of building and shipping production systems. But as a tool to help students tackle more interesting and complex networking problems, I am willing to suspend disbelief. There is also a good argument for using open source models and shared research infrastructure especially given the dubious financial position of the AI model giants. I was intrigued by a discussion on how one becomes a networking educator. My contribution – I learned by watching and emulating the experts who I was lucky to work with at MIT – was not entirely satisfactory to me, and I continue to ponder this question. For one thing, I never had to supervise grad students myself, so there are some definite holes in my experience (which are growing in the “AI era”). An interview with me conducted in 2020 by SIGCOMM chair Matt Caesar, who generously calls me a great educator, contains a few ideas, but this seems like a topic we need to invest more time in, especially as we think about what extra materials need to accompany our next book. What remains at the core? Larry and I joined a breakout to discuss the questions: “What should remain at the core of networking education? Which traditional topics should we keep, and which should we rethink?” Larry started the discussion with the motivating example of QUIC, which is new enough, and complex enough, that it’s missing from a lot of introductory networking courses. His position (which I share) is that a student encountering QUIC for the first time should be able to make sense of it, by relating it to other things they already understand (like reliable transmission, congestion control, and end-to-end security). And from that it follows that we need to teach students enough about the underlying principles of networking and system architecture so that they can make sense of a new thing and fit it into their mental model. This brings us back to the centrality of understanding system design as a discipline, not just learning the details of the existing artifacts. We use the artifacts to illustrate principles at work

events.title: Katherine promised new $13.3m levee after town's worst flood in 28 years
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts NT government commits $13.3 million from Flood Recovery Fund to build Katherine South levee Katherine's levee was designed to divert floodwater away from the town centre, with extra funding now committed to enhancing local flood mitigation strategies. ( ABC News: James Elton ) Residents in the regional Northern Territory town of Katherine have welcomed a $13.3 million government promise to build a new levee following recent devastating floods. Road raising works are also planned, with funding to come from both the NT and federal governments. It is not yet clear how long it will take to deliver the 3-kilometre long project, but it is expected to feature 1.6-metre high dirt embankments and a 1.5-metre high levee wall. Months on from the worst flooding Katherine has seen in almost three decades, the regional Northern Territory town has been promised a new multi-million-dollar levee. The Katherine River recorded its highest flood peak since 1998 in March this year, with authorities at the time describing the Top End's extreme weather as "back-to-back, compounding, concurrent, consecutive events within a four-month period", including two tropical cyclones in a single wet season. In a statement released today by Flood Recovery Minister and local member, Jo Hersey, the NT government announced $13.3 million had been earmarked for the construction of a 3-kilometre long flood levee in Katherine South. In early March, workers in Katherine could be seen installing metal rails across several roads to establish the levee. ( ABC News: James Elton ) With funds drawn from the NT's $100m Flood Recovery Fund , established during the March floods, a spokesperson for the Country Liberal Party (CLP) government said the new levee would help protect "an additional 210 homes and businesses" in Katherine South. "Once complete, the combined function of the Katherine north and south levees will provide greater flood protection for Katherine residents, mitigating flood impacts up to a one in 20-year flood event," they said. Trent de With, a local volunteer who has supported Katherine's flood recovery efforts, said the levee would be "very advantageous to the people who live on that side of town". Trent de With was among the army of local volunteers who stepped in to support flood-affected homes and businesses in Katherine earlier this year. ( ABC News: James Elton ) Mr de With said after the March floods, stagnant water sat in some Katherine South streets "for the longest period out of anywhere". The plan features a wall levee and earth embankments. ( Supplied: NT government ) The government says the Katherine South levee will extend "from the western side of the Katherine Country Club in Pearce Street, to the southern tip of Katherine South on the Victoria Highway". The levee is expected to feature new 1.6-metre high dirt embankments and a 1.5-metre tall levee wall, plus road raising works on Murphy Street, Murray Street and Bicentennial Road. It is not yet clear how long the southern levee will take to deliver, or when construction will begin. NT funds bolster federal commitment Katherine Town Council Mayor Joanna Holden said locals were feeling positive about today's announcement. The NT government has committed millions of dollars to expand Katherine's flood mitigation strategy, months on from the town's worst flooding in almost three decades. ( ABC News: James Elton ) Cr Holden said the federal government had previously promised $9.1m , but the extra NT government funding could help deliver "a better outcome" for Katherine than initially expected. The mayor said while "the council at this stage hasn't been engaged in a great deal of the planning", she wanted to ensure the project did not come at a cost to ratepayers or local infrastructure. Joanna Holden has welcomed the $13.3 million NT government commitment, hoping it can save Katherine South from future floods. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) Cr Holden said the new levee could potentially divert more water to the Katherine showgrounds, where there were buildings and "a lot of electrical outlets", so the council was keen to weigh in on the plan. "This year, the water remained there for a significant period of time after the flooding and that obviously in itself — having water sitting there — creates more issues," she said. Floodwater overwhelmed the local levee and spilled into Katherine's CBD in early March. ( ABC News: James Elton ) Mr de With said he hoped the new infrastructure would push future floodwater further back from residential streets.

events.title: London buses in decline? Why public transport in global cities is slowing to a crawl – visualised
events.summary: As experts fear for future of UK capital’s bus network, some commuters are giving up entirely. London is not alone – with worrying implications for the poorest in society Few things say London more than a red double-decker. But the capital’s buses have a problem: they are getting slower. In congested streets, services are being squeezed. And for the millions of people who rely on buses, more than any other form of London transport, journeys are ever longer. On the 22 , a route through some of the busiest streets in the capital towards Oxford Circus, it’s easy to see why. Buses regularly get stuck in stop-start traffic… Strings of red lights frequently slow buses down… And roadworks restrict the space in which buses can operate.… In 2025, the 22 was the second slowest bus in London, averaging just under 6mph. This is 16% slower than its average speed a decade ago. Back then, today’s hour-long journey would have taken 51 minutes. When the Guardian sent a reporter on the bus on a June morning, the bus was stationary for 40 out of the 108 minutes it took to reach Oxford Circus. This is a pattern seen across the UK capital. In the west, the 207 to White City is 14% slower than a decade ago, with an average speed of 7.4mph in 2025. That’s slower than the average beginner cyclist. The 243 to Waterloo , connecting north London to the city centre, slowed down by 5% . One of the city’s most popular routes, these slower journeys were taken by 9.8 million passengers in 2025. These routes are three examples of wider, continuing trend across London – and indeed, other cities across the world. Buses are slow, and they’re getting slower. Percentage change in average speed in 2025 versus 2015. This map shows how 578 of the 700 London bus routes have seen their average speed reduced in the past decade. Experts warn that slower buses risk driving passengers away: research cited by Transport for London (TfL) suggests a 10% fall in speed leads to a 6% drop in demand. Passenger journeys in London have already fallen by more than 300m a year, or 16%, since 2013, despite the city’s population growing by almost a million people. The city’s mayor, Sadiq Khan, does not play down the issue. “We’re really concerned about bus usage. One of the reasons, when you speak to commuters, is a lack of reliability. And why is it they lack reliability? Because of bus speed.” A congested city, with ever more demands on road space, has left London facing difficult choices over which modes of transport to prioritise. But when passengers turn away from slower buses, the service frequencies and even routes are liable to be cut. The fear is, as one industry figure puts it, “a vicious circle of decline”: slower buses; fewer passengers; and increasing pressure on services. Recent research has also pointed to this trend being recorded in other global cities such as Paris, Brussels, Lisbon and beyond. The growing wait for the London bus – in data Guardian analysis of data from TfL, which runs London’s road and rail public transport network, reveals several indicators that the capital’s bus services have slowed, become truncated or less reliable. The Covid-19 pandemic had a sharp and obvious impact on the data, but there are clear downwards trends cutting through that period. Across the network as a whole, the average speed in 2025-26 stood at 9.18mph – the lowest speed since comparable records began in 2013-14, and a 4.8% drop over this period. Bus timetables have long been adjusted to reflect London’s traffic. A snapshot of routes analysed by the economist Alexander Jan, a veteran of transport planning in the capital, found scheduled journey times are now, on average, 30% longer than they were 50 years ago. Yet even with that extra time built in, buses are increasingly failing to meet expectations. Delays have worsened: on high-frequency routes – those running more than five buses an hour – passengers now wait 22% longer than expected, up from 18% in 2018. If unreliability is, as Khan argues, deterring passengers, the latest ridership figures are concerning. Last year saw the first fall in bus journeys since the post-pandemic recovery. Between 2010 and 2019, annual passenger numbers consistently exceeded 2 billion; in 2024, they fell to 1.8 billion. At the same time, the size of London’s bus network has shrunk. Between 2010 and 2019, TfL buses travelled an average of 487m km (303m miles) a year. Over the past three years, that figure has fallen to about 460m. Across the network buses are slower, passenger numbers are falling, services cover fewer miles and waiting times are rising. Those slower journeys come with a financial cost. Because drivers’ wages account for the largest share of operating costs, slower buses mean more vehicles and more staff are needed to provide the same level of service.

events.title: Mum’s Alzheimer’s has trapped the kids’ NatWest cash
events.summary: A First Saver account was set up by my mother when the children were born which we planned to use to fund them through university My mother set up NatWest First Saver accounts for my children when they were born. The accounts are held in trust for when they turn 18 and my parents have paid into them monthly to help fund them through university. My mother is now in the final stages of Alzheimer’s and I have registered financial power of attorney for her. My daughter began university last year and my son starts this month, but I have been unable to access the £20,000 in their respective accounts. I was told my mother has to give consent for the children to access them, but she’s not in a position to do so. I’ve been variously advised to set up online banking in my mother’s name without her consent, to request a one-off payment of less than £1,000 and, upsettingly, that it would be easier if my mother were dead. As a consequence, we’ve had to take out a bank loan to cover my daughter’s expenses. SW, Worcestershire NatWest blames “lack of colleague awareness” of a “complex process”. We’re talking here of numerous colleagues in call centres and in branches who, over the best part of a year, have been unable to fathom what should be a standard procedure. This appears to be a training issue and it’s hardly reassuring that “learning from your experience” will be used to “inform future improvements”. Your children now have access to their funds and compensation has been paid to reflect the delays. We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. events.title: Former treasurer says economic reform in Australia will take 'financial crisis'
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Former treasurer says Australia needs 'financial crisis' for economic reform to happen Topic: Business, Economics and Finance Former treasurer Joe Hockey says voters will not back meaningful fiscal reform unless there is a "financial crisis". He says a major problem is government spending with "no restraint" in order to be re-elected. As global interest rates rise, governments are under pressure to reduce spending. With federal government debt surpassing $1 trillion, and future generations bearing the burden of the growing interest bill, the clamour for budget repair is growing. But last night, Australian treasurers past and present delivered some insight into the difficulty of getting any kind form of meaningful reform across the line, one before an audience of power brokers and the other on ABC's The Business. Joe Hockey, former treasurer in the Abbott Coalition government, knows full well the difficulty of introducing any kind of fiscal reform. In his first budget, shortly after coming to power in 2013, Mr Hockey up-ended a raft of assurances during the election campaign with a series of wide-ranging spending cuts and user pay fees that enraged the electorate. The Abbott government ended up backing away from most of the swingeing cuts in the face of that opposition. When asked by The Business host Kirsten Aiken whether any meaningful fiscal reform was even possible if it cost voters money, his answer was an emphatic "no". "And people will only take the medicine when they, you know, feel really ill about it. And I think this is coming right across the world." 'Whatever it takes to get re-elected' His sentiments were echoed by current Treasurer Jim Chalmers in his address to an Australian Financial Review gathering on Tuesday. Jim Chalmers says debt and deficits are escalating worldwide. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts. ) Mr Hockey pointed to an inflection point occurring across the developed world in government finances where income tax, the biggest source of government income, is about to be exceeded by welfare payments. "The problem is governments have no restraint when it comes to expenditure," he said. "They're so focused on populism, they'll spend whatever it takes to get re-elected and that's particularly acute now that … one side of government isn't getting 50 per cent of the votes." The fragmenting of political parties and voting patterns has made the task even more difficult as temporary coalitions of divergent parties are formed. "You're going to be populist because you're trying to win the votes of some minority over there," Mr Hockey said. The phenomenon may now be more acute, but it certainly is not new. As treasurer, Mr Hockey philosophically was more aligned with the school of thought pushing for lower taxes and less spending. He oversaw the dismantling of a key aspect of the Henry tax reforms by abolishing the resources rent tax and the carbon tax, which significantly reduced the federal government's tax haul. When combined with his ditched spending cuts, the end result was a decade of deficits during the greatest resources boom in Australian history. Earlier this week, Mr Chalmers delivered the seventh and latest Intergenerational Report, which laid out the challenges of ever delivering a balanced budget over the long term. Young Australians face tough future In 40 years, with an estimated population of 40 million, Australia will be more indebted and face what increasingly appears to be a permanent budget deficit. An aging population with ever greater costs associated with health and aged care and with a smaller proportion of workers supporting them points to an ongoing and possibly permanent structural deficit. Yesterday, the treasurer pointed to the escalating debt and ongoing deficits amongst the world's most powerful economies, which in recent months have sent global interest rates higher, adding to the already substantial financial strains. "We are not entirely powerless in the face of all this," he said. "We have advantages, we are better placed and better prepared and we have a better plan than other countries. All four major banks and the bulk of money market traders believe the Reserve Bank will raise interest rates next week and governor Michele Bullock did nothing to dissuade them during a speech in Sydney. "But the point remains that something as consequential as the world's ability to finance its budgets is, to some degree, hostage to decisions taken in Washington and on Wall Street." It was a point that Mr Hockey concurred with. "You can't keep borrowing hoping that it'll just go away. And the United States is no different.

events.title: Residents near huge data centre demand financial compensation
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts AI data centres probed by Senate inquiry as locals near NextDC facility demand compensation NextDC's M3 site in West Footscray spans 41,000 square metres. ( ABC News: Kyle Harley ) Residents near a major data centre in Melbourne's west are demanding remediation and financial compensation, including voluntary home buybacks. The Victorian government yesterday unveiled a strategy for data centre construction in the state, which will not apply to data centres already built or in the pipeline. A Senate inquiry into the impact of AI and data centres on Australian communities will hold its final day of hearings on October 1. Residents living just metres from a sprawling, hyper-scale data centre in Melbourne's west have called for remediation and financial compensation over the ongoing impacts of pollution and potential fire risk. It comes as a Senate inquiry on artificial intelligence and data centres today heard from residents and local councils about the impact of an influx of data centres in Melbourne's west and north. The Victorian government yesterday unveiled new regulations to ban data centres near homes and schools, including 150-metre buffer zones, while mandating the use of renewable energy and non-drinking water. But the rules would not be applied retrospectively , meaning projects that had already been approved or had lodged planning applications would not need to abide by the updated standards. The Victorian government argues data centre development will lead to job creation and investment. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) Tech giant NextDC's West Footscray data centre is located just 15 metres from homes. An application to more than double the facility's size, lodged earlier this year, would not need to meet the new regulations if approved. Another data centre, the Perri Melbourne Data Centre (PMDC), was approved by the planning minister last year and will also be situated in West Footscray, just a block away from NextDC. Advocacy group Citizens for Tottenham, which represents people living in the suburbs of West Footscray, Tottenham and Kingsville, called for remediation, arguing Victoria's new rules were "too little too late". Among their chief complaints are fumes and noise pollution emitted by dozens of back-up diesel generators at the NextDC data centre, which are run regularly for maintenance . Call for voluntary buybacks, compensation The group wants residents living within 500 metres of the data centres to be offered a voluntary buyback based on the latest Maribyrnong City Council rates notice or independent market valuation, whichever is higher. Stamp duty and moving costs would also be covered, while households would also receive a one-off payment of $10,000 to assist with time off work for moving and "general inconvenience". Sean Brown is a founding member of the Citizens of Tottenham, a community group which is opposed NextDC's expansion. ( ABC News: Kyle Harley ) "Many people don't want to live near [the data centre], but it's not going anywhere," Citizen for Tottenham member Sean Brown told the ABC, adding that 760 homes and 2,500 residents were within 500 metres. Research released in July by Australian software firm Airteam and Primara estimated that having a data centre located in close proximity could wipe up to $35,000 from a property's price. The survey of 1,000 Australians found 83 per cent of respondents would refuse to buy a home near a data centre without a price discount. Mr Brown said residents who stayed in the area should also be entitled to compensation for loss of amenity during construction, including $5,000 per year for households located at the boundary of the NextDC or PMDC facilities. He said compensation should be funded by data centre operators or the state government, and that local residents were also considering legal action. NextDC and PMDC developer Perri Projects were contacted for comment. Sarah Hanson-Young argues only AI firms are benefiting from data centre development at present. ( ABC News: Adam Kennedy ) Senate inquiry chair and Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young backed calls for impacted residents to be compensated by tech companies. "Australians need to get something out of this," Senator Hanson-Young said. "Compensation should be on the table, but it's also about what is the community benefit from these big AI facilities? "Right now, the only ones benefiting are the big, trillion-dollar AI companies," she said. The Victorian government argues data centre development will lead to job creation and investment, pointing to $5.8 billion in capital expenditure from the sector last year.

events.title: Incredible Holdings files application for judicial management
events.summary: An automatic moratorium, which commenced on Sept 21, will be in effect until the court rules on the application. SINGAPORE – Catalist-listed Incredible Holdings has filed a Singapore High Court application to place the company under judicial management, it said on Sept 23. The application, filed two days ago, proposed the appointment of Ellyn Tan Huixian and Terrence Chin Khee Loon of Forvis Mazars Consulting as joint and several judicial managers of the electronics and consumer goods company. Incredible Holdings on Sept 19 said that one of its independent directors, Eunice Veon Koh Pei Lee, was assisting in investigations by the Commercial Affairs Department and the Monetary Authority of Singapore. The investigations involve alleged offences under the Securities and Futures Act (Chapter 289) and Securities and Futures Act 2001. On Sept 21 , Incredible Holdings said that Koh had told the company she understood that she was asked only to assist with investigations and was not their subject. The company last held an annual general meeting in 2023 and has not convened meetings for the financial periods ended June 2024 and June 2025, placing it in breach of listing rules. An automatic moratorium, which commenced on Sept 21 , will be in effect until the court rules on the judicial management application. Under the moratorium, no order may be made and no resolution may be passed for the winding up of the company. No step may be taken to enforce any security over any company property, or to repossess any goods, except with the permission of the court. No other proceedings may also be commenced or continued against Incredible Holdings during this period, except with the permission of the court and subject to such terms as the court may impose. Additionally, no enforcement order or other legal process may be issued, continued or executed, and no distress may be levied, against the company or its property, except with the permission of the court. Incredible Holdings added that it will release further announcements as and when there are material developments in this matter. THE BUSINESS TIMES

events.title: ‘You should not be here,' Trump tells CNN at UN as standoff with media outlets persists
events.summary: A tense moment between President Donald Trump and CNN's Kaitlan Collins is a stark reminder of how the conflict between the administration and some news outlets has escalated in just a few days NEW YORK -- On a day of high-stakes diplomacy on the global stage, President Donald Trump began his United Nations visit by telling a prominent U.S. journalist, “You should not be here.” “It’s an honor to be here,” Trump said as he entered U.N. doors Tuesday ahead of his speech to the General Assembly and faced Kaitlan Collins of CNN , a frequent target of his ire. “I’m surprised that CNN is here covering me. You should not be here covering me. You said you weren’t going to cover me.” As Collins noted later on air, CNN said nothing of the kind. The administration had banned CNN from White House grounds days earlier — along with MS NOW and Politico — and removed the network from pool duty. But CNN had been admitted into the U.N. as regularly credentialed media. In any case, the tense moment was a stark reminder of how dramatically the bitter conflict between Trump and news outlets whose coverage he objects to as “fake news" has escalated in just a few days. The current ban was the subject of a joint lawsuit filed Monday by the three outlets, calling the decision selective — based on the content of their coverage — and asking a judge to find Trump's move unconstitutional. Late Tuesday, the administration filed a response urging the court to reject the news outlets' request, saying “access to the White House is a privilege — not a right.” The government argued that White House officials can control journalists’ access to “restricted presidential areas,” such as the Oval Office. “Significantly, Presidents have long decided which journalists should receive privileged access, which has varied substantially by administration,” they wrote. A hearing is scheduled for Wednesday afternoon. On Tuesday, Trump doubled down on his remarks and said negative coverage was dangerous for the country. Asked whether he would allow the outlets back in if the court rules against the White House, he said, “Well, it probably will, because this is a judge who’s not a particularly fair judge.” He was referring to U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, whom he appointed in 2017 and who ordered a CNN journalist’s access restored in a similar case in 2018. “So you never know,” Trump added. "I think we have a right to clean out fake news." Trump’s comments echoed others he's made since announcing the ban Friday. He has referred to “purposely negative stories” as justification for the ban. The ban and lawsuit are part of a long-running conflict between the president — especially in his second term — and media outlets he finds unfavorable. Trump has responded in the courtroom, or with regulatory action. He's also lashed out at individual reporters in person or over social media, sometimes in strikingly personal terms — as he has with CNN's Collins, most recently in a speech at the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner . On air, after her exchange with Trump on Tuesday, Collins said: “We never said we were not going to cover the president. We will do our best to cover him each and every day.” Tuesday began with an item missing from the daily press schedule issued by the White House: It did not list the U.S. network pool, a departure from the norm. CNN had been the designated pool network for the president’s trip to New York, according to a schedule that divides coverage of certain events between the five major networks. But Trump's ban removed it from pool duties. Cindy Crawford's son Presley Gerber dies at 27 Hunter charged with manslaughter in shooting of woman he mistook for a deer: Police Twin sisters conjoined at head underwent successful separation surgery: Hospital The other pool members agreed, in solidarity, not to replace CNN with another network on the coverage, and further to suspend all pool coverage until further notice. Other news outlets also took steps in solidarity. The Associated Press joined a number of news organizations, including The Washington Post and The New York Times, in a decision not to publish photographs of presidential events Monday. It remains to be seen how long both the ban and the collective media action will continue. In speeches and meetings Tuesday, Trump was seen plenty by global audiences, thanks to UNTV — the official United Nations broadcast arm — and pool journalists covering other international leaders. Meanwhile, a sign was spotted in the White House workspace: “I stand with AP, CNN, MS NOW, Politico.” One longtime TV analyst says the lack of constant coverage will prove damaging to a spotlight-loving president — which may be one reason the standoff ultimately ends. “This ban is not going to go on forever because he doesn’t want that to happen, any more than anybody else,” said Robert Thompson, director of Syracuse University’s Bleier Center for Television and Popular Culture.

events.title: Burnham navigates diplomatic rapids in first Trump meeting, but turbulent waters lie ahead
events.summary: British aides express relief, as the prime minister’s team say the meeting was at the ‘top end of their expectations’ On the flight out to New York this week, one of Andy Burnham’s senior aides warned him that meeting Donald Trump would be the political equivalent of white water rafting. While there is a well-known playbook the US president deploys when he first meets other world leaders, he remains a deeply unpredictable figure and any dealings with him can leave you crashing into the rocks. Trump’s strategy involves personal flattery, transactional diplomacy and a public evaluation of his guest’s skills. When Keir Starmer first met the president at the White House early last year, it was there in spades. Trump praised his “beautiful” accent, said that Britain was a “wonderful” place and claimed that he had driven a “hard bargain” on tariffs. On the flight home, the clearly relieved former prime minister gave journalists a Trump-style thumbs up, telling them he was “happy” before returning to the front of the plane. But in time, their relationship fell apart . Just over 18 months later, it was an apprehensive Burnham’s turn to head down the diplomatic rapids at the UN general assembly. As the new prime minister faced the press after their talks, the president again deployed the playbook – describing Burnham as a “natural businessperson” who had “lots of assets on his side”, while predicting he would be a “great” leader. The British side, including foreign secretary Ed Miliband and national security adviser Jonathan Powell, could not hide their relief when Trump kept his policy differences with the UK muted – beyond inevitable criticism of what he described as the “terrible” Chagos deal. Even on the issue that fully ruptured Starmer’s relationship with Trump – his refusal to allow the US to use British airbases for attacks against Iran at the start of the war – the president held his punches. “Some countries could have stepped forward. But there aren’t too many countries, frankly, that could have handled that,” he said. Afterwards, British officials – even those who have witnessed the Trump strategy in action before and knew it would not necessarily last – were delighted with how the talks had gone. “It was the top end of our expectations,” said one. “All the issues you guys had written about – the Falklands, a united Ireland, Chagos – all fine.” They admitted the West Bank settlement trade ban was the one area they had worried about most. But a summer of diplomacy got Trump on board, and to their relief, he deferred to Burnham on the question. “It was a bit of a curveball, but it was better than him criticising it,” another aide said. Burnham even managed to use the moment to steer the raft – briefly – into calmer waters, explaining his hopes of drawing an end to the political turbulence that has gripped Britain for more than a decade, and creating a more “positive story” for the country instead. “More than anything, we just needed them to connect, and start building a relationship that we can leverage when we need to,” a third government official said. But just as Starmer found that with time, policy differences between the UK and US made the relationship more difficult to navigate, so his successor is likely to find the same. Burnham’s team is right to be cautious about the unsteadiness that Trump can inflict – his international actions causing ripples in the UK too. The prime minister may have survived the first set of diplomatic rapids, but there are more to navigate ahead.

events.title: Qantas announces 18-hour direct flights from Sydney to New York with onboard ‘wellbeing zones’
events.summary: Due to take off in 2028, it is set to be the national carrier’s second ultra long-haul route after Sydney to London Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Qantas says travellers will be able to fly between Sydney and New York in just 18 hours from mid-2028 when the airline launches its second ultra long-haul route, cutting at least three hours from the travel time. The route will be the second in Qantas’ Project Sunrise expansion plans, with new Sydney to London direct flights planned for October 2027, after some delays. It would be the first commercial direct flight from Kingsford-Smith airport to New York’s JFK airport. Qantas currently offers flights from Sydney to New York with a stopover in Los Angeles, which take 21 hours and typically cost more than $1,400 one way or more than $1,900 return. Qantas has not disclosed prices for the Project Sunrise routes. It has previously suggested direct fares could cost 20% more than stopover fares and said ticket prices are facing upward pressure . Tickets for the Sydney to New York route are set to go on sale in August 2027, Qantas said. It has not specified which month flights will begin. When it announced the London route launch date, the company said it would reveal launch timings in 2027. Qantas is planning to unveil more 20-hour direct flights from Perth in future but has abandoned references to previous hopes to run routes from Brisbane or Melbourne. The Project Sunrise flights’ initial launch date of 2022 was delayed by the Covid-19 pandemic. Subsequent plans to start in 2025 , then early 2027 , were waylaid by manufacturing delays at Airbus, Qantas has said. The company has ordered 12 Airbus A350–1000ULRs, fitted with extra fuel tanks, which can fly over 16,000km and up to 22 hours nonstop. The first is expected to arrive in Australia in April 2027. The planes were specifically designed to fly up to 22 hours nonstop for Qantas, to complete some of the longest commercial flights in the world. A test model in July completed a 24-hour, 24-minute flight from Melbourne to Airbus’s manufacturing facility in Toulouse, France, believed to be the longest-ever commercial flight. Each plane will contain a dedicated “wellbeing zone” between the economy and premium economy cabins, where passengers will be able to stretch, watch guided exercise videos and help themselves to snacks and drinks. Only 140 of the A350–1000ULR’s 238 seats are standard economy. It contains six first-class suites, 52 business suites and 40 premium economy seats. Get the most important news as it breaks The company expects the Project Sunrise flights and sustained premium flight demand to increase its earnings by $400m over the next five years, with profit margins to rise from today’s rate of 4% to 10%. Qantas said demand for its flights in and out of New York have doubled since 2023. Short-term US arrivals to Australia picked up 4% in the year to July 2026 compared with the year prior, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics. However, Australians travelling and returning from the US dropped 9% in the same period. Qantas’s chief executive, Vanessa Hudson, unveiled the start date at a launch party in a New York cocktail bar, as world leaders gathered in the city for the United Nations general assembly. Hudson said the flights could change the way Australians travel. “Reaching New York nonstop completes a vision we set out many years ago, and it’s a moment of enormous pride for the thousands of our people who have been working hard to make Project Sunrise a reality,” she said. The company is training pilots on its A350 simulator and is teaching engineers about the new aircraft. It said more than 360 pilots and 1,200 cabin crew will be trained to operate the aircraft by the time the entire fleet has arrived.

events.title: Europe’s top private markets firm EQT sets up first Middle East base in Abu Dhabi
events.summary: EQT, Europe’s largest private markets investment firm, is setting up its first Middle East office in Abu Dhabi’s financial centre, ADGM, joining a growing roster of global asset managers expanding in the emirate. The firm, which manages $389 billion in client assets, will use Abu Dhabi as the base for its new Middle East platform as it seeks investment opportunities across the Gulf, EQT said. The expansion reflects the “distinct priorities and market dynamics” across the Gulf and wider Middle East, with EQT planning to build out its regional platform over time. “The launch of EQT's Middle East platform reflects our conviction in the scale and momentum of opportunity across the GCC,” said Per Franzen, chief executive and managing partner at EQT, referring to the Gulf Co-operation Council. “We see significant opportunities to support the growth of our existing portfolio companies and invest in new businesses across sectors undergoing structural transformation and attracting long-term capital.” EQT's global sector expertise and company-building capabilities can contribute “meaningfully to the GCC's long-term economic development”, he added. Growing roaster EQT’s entry on the ADGM roster follows $315 billion private credit provider Blue Owl’s move to set up a base in Abu Dhabi in June. The two are among several alternative investment managers who have chosen the emirate as a base, underscoring its continued appeal for global asset managers and financial giants despite war-driven uncertainties. The UAE, like its Gulf and wider Middle Eastern peers, initially faced waves of missile and drone attacks from Tehran after the breakout of the US and Israel's war with Iran on February 28. However, the conflict, now in its seventh month, has not deterred international financial firms from setting up an operational base in Abu Dhabi. A base in the UAE capital provides global investors and money managers with opportunities to expand regional operations and work closely with some of the world's largest sovereign wealth funds, as well as large family offices and institutional partners. EQT said the ADGM base will help deepen engagement with investors, companies and partners” across the wider Gulf markets. The Gulf region is increasingly playing an important role in global capital flows and economic growth, supported by the ambitious national development agendas of the member states. These development goals of Gulf nations “align closely with EQT’s long-standing thematic investment approach, active ownership model, as well as its expertise in digital and AI infrastructure investments, the company said. EQT’s Middle East platform is led by Jimmy Mahtani, who has been appointed chairman of Gulf operations, in addition to his role as chairman of South and South-East Asia for EQT Private Capital. The ADGM office is led by Smiyet Belrhiti, who has been appointed senior executive officer. With the addition of Abu Dhabi, EQT now has offices in more than 25 countries that together account for more than 80 per cent of global economic output. “Across the Middle East, we are seeing a growing pool of high-quality companies in sectors central to EQT’s long-term strategies,” said Mr Belrhiti, who also runs the company’s Middle East operations. With the region’s potential to “produce globally significant companies over the next decade”, the company is committed to being a long-term partner in that journey, he added.
