events.title: Cautious farmers embrace renewable energy to boost income streams
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Farmers warm to renewables but concerns over large-scale land impacts remain A wind farm project is being investigated in South Australia. ( ABC News: Craig Heerey ) Economic incentives are starting to show signs of outweighing farmers' scepticism about renewables. Smaller-scale projects are winning farmers over, while large-scale wind and transmission infrastructure can still face resistance. Experts expect to see a greater shift towards renewables as economic benefits strengthen. Farmers who have long been wary of hosting renewable energy on their land are showing signs of warming to the idea, as government incentives and economic benefits start to chip away at old scepticism. Renewable energy advocates hope continued education, along with grants and other financial incentives, will encourage more farmers to embrace renewable projects. Energy experts say there is plenty of room for farms to grow their income from renewables or use them to power their own operations. Bridget Johnson, whose family breeds cattle across two properties in South Australia's Upper South East, has signed up to a wind project planned for the Willalooka district, hoping to diversify her family's income. Bridget Johnson with daughter Edwina on the family farm. ( Supplied: Bridget Johnson ) It was not a decision the Johnsons took lightly, with the whole family needing to come to a consensus. "I think it's easy to make a decision based on perception or bias, and for us it was really important to have facts and information," Ms Johnson said. Diversified income stream for farmers The research they did changed how the family viewed the project, with the positives for the project outweighing the negatives. She said having an additional revenue stream in agriculture that was not dependent on traditional climatic and market drivers was something the Johnsons saw as a sustainable model for their business and family moving forward. "Most farmers will absolutely appreciate having a recurring income that's not tied to the rain or to the price at the sale yards or the price that you're receiving for your livestock," she said. "It's an exceptionally important part of our business going forward." Bridget Johnson with her parents, Ian and Louise Johnson. The whole family agreed to embrace renewable energy opportunities. ( Supplied: Bridget Johnson ) The company behind the project, Voyager Renewables, is consulting with landholders before it undertakes studies on how the project can affect land and groundwater. These impacts can often be the sticking point for farmers. "Do we go very early with very little information, or do we go later in the process with lots of information?" Closing the renewable communication gap University of Southern Queensland senior lecturer in electrical and electronic engineering Md Alamgir Hossain had observed growing interest from farmers in smaller-scale renewables, where the benefits were clearer and the impact on the land was smaller. Md Alamgir Hossain has been observing a slow change in farmers' attitudes to renewables. ( Supplied: Dr Md Alamgir Hossain ) Dr Hossain said the larger projects were a tougher sell. "The majority of them probably are anti-renewable energy infrastructure such as the big transmission line or a commercial-scale wind farm," he said. Dr Hossain said the key to winning farmers over was being up-front about the impact renewables could have on the land, including whether new roads, power lines and other physical infrastructure would need to be installed. "There is a communication gap. We need transparency, and we need clear engagement with the farmer so that we can convey the evidence-based support," he said. "We can consult with them so that daily operation of the farming is not hampered or less hampered." Solar costs for business to be slashed under energy scheme expansion The federal government is set to announce changes to the Small-scale Renewable Energy scheme in a bid to help businesses install solar systems and close the gap with residential take-up. Earlier this year, the federal government expanded the Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme (SRES), a move Dr Hossain believed would encourage farmers to consider larger renewable projects on their properties. "For the medium farms, this is the opportunity for them to install or to observe how renewable energy can give benefits on their farm to electrifying the current machineries or stationary equipment," he said. "At the same time, they are going toward more energy independence.

events.title: DRC prime minister defends Ebola response
events.summary: The prime minister of the Democratic Republic of Congo rejected framing the country’s relations with Washington as solely based around minerals, and offered a frank account of the cause of early Ebola cases remaining undetected. The relationship is a broad economic partnership spanning infrastructure, energy, and local processing of minerals, not just extraction and export, Judith Suminwa said at Semafor’s The Next 3 Billion event in New York. She also said the US is closely watching the Inga hydropower project on the Congo River, noting that a meeting on it will take place next month in Paris with American participants. The World Bank is committing financial support to the Inga 3 Development Program in the country. On Ebola, Suminwa said through a translator that cases of the Bundibugyo strain were slow to surface because its malaria-like symptoms “can be interpreted as just a benign disease.” The DRC had reported over 7,000 confirmed cases and 3,600 deaths as of September 20; the Ebola outbreak became the fastest-growing on record in August. The DRC government has committed $50 million to the response, including $3 million for research, with partners mobilizing hundreds of millions of dollars in support, Suminwa said. She added that more is needed so the health system “can be strengthened so we don’t have to face such outbreaks anymore.” — Adrian Elimian

events.summary: The News An AI crisis communications line between the US and China should be a “starting place” for relations between the superpowers on the technology, OpenAI’s head of national security policy said. Sasha Baker said at Semafor’s Next 3 Billion event on Tuesday that she is “cautiously optimistic” about reports that Washington and Beijing are discussing an AI safety notification system, with a special focus on national security concerns. It’s “a great place to start,” she said. “I see that as a starting place, not the ending place. But it’s substantive and real.” She said the US and China have to find common ground because they are home to the world’s leading AI labs, but “every country in the world has a stake in what happens with advanced AI, and we want for those voices to also be represented in the conversation.” OpenAI’s Sam Altman, who has backed calls to pace frontier AI model development, will tell the UN Security Council on Wednesday about the need to “internationalize the conversation around standards” around AI, Baker said. Earlier on Tuesday, US President Donald Trump rejected the idea of international oversight of AI, calling it a “globalist scheme.” He will also relay “the gravity of the moment that we’re in, and a recognition that these models really are displaying capabilities that are strategically significant,” she added. Know More Baker’s remarks came amid concerns that advanced AI models could be turned into potent hacking tools, capable of finding and exploiting unknown security flaws with little human direction. OpenAI earlier this month launched Astra, its first model designated as being “cybercritical.” Baker said there are no current plans to leverage the model to allow the US government to do offensive cybersecurity work, like proactive attacks on adversaries. “We… acknowledge that in the wrong hands it could be used for offensive cyber,” she said. “That is not something that we’re provisioning models for right now.”

events.title: Windows CLOSEDQUORUM malware uses AI models to autonomously select post-compromise actions
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters 'first' publicly documented Windows implant to use LLMs for C2 Shut up and calculate: Jev's new AI primitives for coders 4 hours ago Frontier AI keeps racing despite calls to slow down 11 hours ago NightmareEclipse's latest zero-day leaves Microsoft Defender stuck in the past 18 hours ago Z.ai says sorry for slurping up your code, open sources ZCode 19 hours ago Register reader hit with surprise bill after Microsoft portals disagreed 22 hours ago A new Windows malware called CLOSEDQUORUM can query up to four LLM providers - Google Gemini, DeepSeek, Qwen, and Mistral - to autonomously select from predefined post-compromise actions, including stealing users’ credentials and cryptocurrency wallets. Once deployed, the malware does not require continued commands from a human operator, according to Cisco Talos, which describes it as, to its knowledge, the first publicly documented Windows implant to use this approach for command-and-control (C2). Talos discovered the binary with its new CAIRN (Cognitive Artifact Intelligence Research Network) toolkit for hunting, classifying, and tracking emerging AI-integrated malware, which the security shop also made available as an open source repository on Tuesday. While the threat hunters haven’t observed any in-the-wild deployment of CLOSEDQUORUM, they said that artifacts from the binary link the malware’s developer to postings that date back to 2025 on criminal forums related to carding. After deployment, the Go-based malware delegates its next action to a quorum of LLMs that vote on what it should do next. If the vote is tied, DeepSeek’s vote takes precedence, followed by Qwen, Mistral, and Gemini. “The session is closed; no humans are admitted,” Talos analyst Ryan Fetterman said on Tuesday. “Four models are queried in sequence, their independent verdicts tallied, and the binary acts, based on their judgment.” This type of “effort displacement,” which transfers a phase of the attack from a human operator to AI systems, can compound the speed and scale advantages of an intrusion by removing the human bottleneck, Fetterman added. “Human operators are bound by attention, working hours, and cognitive load,” he wrote in the Tuesday blog. “An AI system capable of executing a phase of the attack chain can continue when the operator is no longer watching. It does not go offline when the attacker sleeps.” The models’ decisions are limited to the pre-defined actions, and they must choose “ONLY executable decisions,” according to a system prompt that Talos’ researchers extracted from the binary. It tells each model: “You are an advanced malware strategist.” And then the models choose what the malware should do from these capability modules: Steal, which simultaneously runs commands to dump LSASS memory for Windows credentials, steal saved browser passwords across Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, and Mozilla Firefox, and extract cryptocurrency wallet data including MetaMask, Exodus, and Ethereum. Inject generates shellcode and then uses process hollowing or Early Bird injection to execute malicious code. Persist establishes persistence on the infected device. Talos believes the developer provides each operator with a customized executable containing that operator’s Discord webhook and LLM API keys, which are injected at compile time. Stolen credentials land in the operator’s Discord channel and are AES-256-GCM encrypted with a daily rotating key that the operator derives from the message timestamp. According to Fetterman, the “most useful detection strategy” is to look at behavioral characteristics, not domain blocking. “Legitimate applications may contact DeepSeek, OpenRouter, Mistral, Gemini, or Discord independently,” he wrote. “Far fewer should contact several of them while also accessing LSASS, injecting into suspended processes, or creating WMI persistence.

He does not perform well in formal settings, like chambers of government, preferring a blingier room, like Mar-a-Lago, or an outdoor rally. For years, he has made no secret of his hostility to the UN, and the very principles of international order that define it. events.title: New EU industry rules would damage UK, warns Burnham
events.summary: Andy Burnham has warned that planned EU rules to help European manufacturers would damage the UK, as he met European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. The proposals aim to protect EU industry from Chinese competitors by giving companies inside the bloc priority for public contracts and subsidies. The prime minister said he was concerned about how British industry and supply chains could be affected, and raised the subject with von der Leyen when he met her during a UN summit in New York. Speaking on the flight to the US, Burnham also declined to rule out committing to rejoining the EU in Labour's next manifesto, saying it was an issue "for another day". He said his immediate priority was to rebuild the relationship with the EU and reach an agreement that would boost the British economy. The Made In Europe scheme - formally called the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) - is yet to be finalised, but the EU's car industry has called for the UK to be included to prevent disruption to its supply chains. Tensions over the proposed scheme have reportedly further delayed this year's planned EU-UK summit, which had already been postponed in the wake of Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as prime minister in July. Burnham said: "We have considerable support among the member states for the position we are taking, because Europe's argument is not with us. "We both suffer the same effects as other countries, particularly steel and the issue it raises for the steel industry in Europe and in Britain. "We are making the argument 'we are not your enemies here… we are not the problem'. Made in Europe is dealing with a different problem. "We are making the argument that 'let's avoid collateral damage'." Burnham expects to find 'common ground' with Trump in first meeting Published 1 day ago Watch: What to expect from the UN General Assembly Published 1 day ago Ten years on, Brexit's economic impact is becoming clearer Published 14 September Burnham told reporters his own speech to the UN General Assembly later would reflect on the decade since the Brexit vote and the "turbulence comes when outside actors seek to manipulate, to distort facts, influence the British democratic process". "Going into the next decade, we need to be clear-eyed about that and become stronger and more on the front foot about challenging that," he said. Asked if he would rule out making a pledge to rejoin the EU at the next general election, Burnham said: "Our focus at the moment is on a UK-EU summit which we hope will take place later this year. "My immediate priority is to build on the good work that Keir [Starmer] did in rebuilding bridges, because those bridges were broken in the early part of this decade." He added: "What we have got to do is now go to the next level in terms of reaching practical agreement that will further boost the British economy, and those issues are the substance of the summit alongside EU requests around youth mobility." He said questions about rejoining the EU were for "another day". Speaking at the Liberal Democrat conference in Brighton on Monday, the EU's new ambassador to the UK was asked whether the UK could rejoin the EU or be granted associate membership. Jukka Salovaara said: "The doors are open but it's very much up to the UK public to identify and decide on its level of ambition when it comes to deepening cooperation with the EU." Last September, Burnham said he would like to see the UK back in the EU in his lifetime. Earlier this year, he said Brexit had been "damaging" but "the last thing we should do right now is re-run those arguments". The EU has recently suggested Canada could become the bloc's first "associate member". Asked if this could be an option for the UK, Burnham said: "The European Union made it clear that that wasn't open to us." events.title: 'Winter is coming': IMF head issues 'warning' over inflation and central bank tightening
events.summary: The global economy has so far shrugged off $100 oil. It won’t forever. “Winter is coming,” Kristalina Georgieva, managing director of the International Monetary Fund said at Semafor’s Next 3 Billion event in New York, warning that prices will keep climbing. The Iran war — and the energy shocks that have accompanied it — has elevated inflation globally since February, leading central banks around the world to raise interest rates. That raised their borrowing costs — the US will spend more money this year paying interest on the national debt than on its military — which leaves less to cushion the economic fallout. While AI has turbocharged economic development globally, counteracting some of the energy shock, the tech falls short of compensating for the full effect of the Strait of Hormuz’s closure. She’s also watching the economic impacts on the real economy. “We should prepare for people being more unhappy,” she said. “Maybe on the street.” She said the IMF doesn’t yet see the demand for AI-related investments crowding out the ability of global governments to borrow, but “it’s possible this becomes a problem so we have to watch it,” she said. While many market economies “have done miracles to reduce their debt levels, to put in place fiscal discipline and shrink spreads for their borrowing. Now what’s happening is interest rates go up, they’re washing away hard-earned gains in emerging markets. So it’s not competition for money, per se, but it’s the punishment for someone else’s sins that emerging markets have to bear,” she said. — Jake Angelo

events.title: Myer posts $276m annual loss on 'weak' consumer spending, ASX edges higher, NAB hit by IT outage — as it happened
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Department store chain Myer has reported a full-year loss of $276 million amid a "material downturn" in consumer sentiment and "weak" discretionary spending. The ASX edged higher, led by mining stocks, with the energy sector lower on the back of falling oil prices. Late in the day, NAB reported a widespread IT outage on its account and trading platforms. Look back on how the session unfolded, plus the day's financial news and insights from our specialist business reporters on our blog. Disclaimer: this blog is not intended as investment advice. ASX 200 : +0.1% to 8,758 points (live values below) ASX 200 (Tue): +0.3% to 8,758 points Australian dollar : -0.2% to 71.01 US cents Asia: Nikkei +1.4%, Hang Seng -0.9% Kospi +0.7% Shanghai -0.6% Wall Street: S & P 500 flat, Dow -0.4% Nasdaq +0.5%, Europe : Dax flat, FTSE -0.3%, Eurostoxx 600 +0.1% Spot gold : -0.4% to $US4,335/ounce Oil : Brent futures -0.6% to $US98.64/barrel, WTI futures -1.2% to $US89.40/barrel Iron ore (Tuesday): -0.6% to $US96.60/tonne Copper (LME): -0.7% to $US14,664/tonne 10-year bonds: US 4.94%, Australia 5.25% Prices current at around 4:15pm AEST Choose what information you see below by using filters That's it for another day on the blog, thanks for your company. Looking ahead, it looks like a quiet night on Wall Street (bearing in mind the markets are generally only one Presidential social media post away from a materially important swing). We'll be back bright an early with all the news from overnight, rolling through the day which will see the important August jobs data released. Just an update on our earlier post regarding NAB's digital banking outage. NAB issued this statement at 5pm AEST (as we were closing the blog): "Most services have now been restored. Some business customers are continuing to experience login issues via NAB Connect, and we're working as quickly as possible to resolve the remaining impacts. "We apologise to customers for the disruption and thank them for their patience and understanding while we continue to restore services." Until next time, missing you already... ASX gains 0.1% on mining rally as banks sold off After starting brightly, the ASX lost a bit of momentum closing just 0.1% higher at 8,758 points. Demand for miners, and particular gold miners, did the heavy lifting, although property trusts also chipped in. Most other sectors, notably technology, energy and the banks were lower. Mining heavyweights BHP, Rio Tinto and Fortescue all gained, with BHP up 1.4%. The gold sub-sector did even better. The biggest players, Newmont and Northern Star rose between 3 and 4%. St Barbara went ex-dividend and fell. Goodman Group (+3%) led the way in the property sector. The banks and insurers were largely sold off. NAB, despite a widespread outage to its accounts and trading platforms was an exception gaining 0.1%. CBA dropped 0.8%, while IAG shed more than 2% after the ACCC opposed its takeover of RACI insurance in WA. All the oil and gas producers ended lower. Woodside dropped 1.7%. The refiners and retailers were also hit by falling oil prices. Tech and telco stocks generally failed to benefit from the Nasdaq's rally in the US. Xero fell 4.7%. The ASX 200's top mover list was mainly populated by gold miners. Defence focussed tech outfit Electro Optic Systems misfired dropping almost 7% to be the worst performing stock on the ASX 200 Toll road operator Atlas Arteria found itself among the cellar dwellers after going ex-dividend this morning. Just a quick peek at the rundown for The Business with Kirsten Aiken tonight. Kirsten will talk to MST energy analyst Saul Kavonic about the latest moves in the oil market and President Trump's support for a ban on diesel exports from the US Wilson Asset Management's Oscar Oberg will discuss AI factory company Firmus's upcoming IPO and valuation and reporter Alex Turner-Cohen looks at Myer's big loss and majority shareholder Solly Lew finally making it to the board That's The Business broadcast Mondays to Thursdays at 8:44pm on ABC News Channel, after the Late News on ABC TV, and anytime on ABC iView . Having enjoyed six winning sessions and a series of record highs, copper looks like it's having a bit of a breather today, weighed down by a stronger US dollar. Benchmark three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange was down 0.7% at $14,651/tonne. The most-traded copper contract on the Shanghai Futures Exchange edged 0.2% lower to $US16,550.57/tonne. Chinese demand had been boosted by buying ahead of smelter shutdowns for the country's public holidays.

events.title: ‘Hold us accountable’ on data centers, Amazon sustainability chief says
events.summary: The News Amazon’s chief sustainability officer said Tuesday the company needed to “do better” on communicating the environmental impact of its vast data center buildout, amid growing opposition to the projects in the US and Europe. “There is a lot of debate, backlash against data centers in this country right now, and one of the things that we’re doing is taking a look at what have we done well and where have we fallen down and what do we need to do better,” Kara Hurst told Semafor’s The Next Three Billion event in New York. “And so, we’re revising a number of our practices. We’re calling for a lot more transparency and accountability because that’s what people in these communities deserve. We’re saying, ‘hold us accountable for our practices,’” Hurst said. Amazon’s carbon footprint grew for the second year in a row in 2025, as the tech giant accelerated its data center buildout, investing $220 billion in capital expenditure in 2026 alone. But local opposition threatens to hinder tech giants’ race to build, with data center projects worth some $68 billion delayed or blocked because of local opposition between April and June this year, according to Data Center Watch. Amazon is looking to publish more metrics tracking its environmental footprint such as the effectiveness of energy and water usage at sites, Hurst said, part of a wider effort to address concerns from environmentalists and communities. Communities where data centers are built should also get a “return on that investment,” Hurst said. “They should get workforce development, they should get upskilling, they should get economic development.” Know More There is currently no national framework in the US requiring hyperscalers to report data centers’ environmental impact. But Hurst said that voluntary reporting has an advantage over mandated disclosure: It lets companies put data out, have scientists test whether the metrics hold up, and revise the methodology if they don’t, rather than locking in a potentially flawed standard. “What we need is to publish data, information that’s science-led, and to publish it quickly and to put it out there and say, ‘Is this the right methodology?’” she said. The data center race has posed a dilemma for sustainability goals globally. An S&P Global assessment of data center companies globally found that just 15 of the 50 firms surveyed received a passing grade signaling that they would be low-carbon and climate-resilient by 2030. Amazon has set a goal to be net-zero carbon by 2040, but Hurst said the firm will likely see emissions rise in the near term as the data center buildout heats up. “We’ve said all along this is not going to be linear,” Hurst said.

events.title: Security firm finds naming AI agents after Seinfeld characters helps bots join the team
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Not that there's anything wrong with it Anthropic decides to support OpenAI's markdown instructions spec 4 days ago If a Mac mini is agentic overkill, try this glowing pyramid that runs personal bots 6 days ago AI agents can modify themselves without humans telling them to do so 6 days ago TypeSafe AI debuts model for machines that plays Doom 7 days ago Hundreds of AI agents helped PaperCut attacker hit 395+ orgs, and some went off script 12 days ago Backslash Security, a four-year-old Tel Aviv-based AI security biz, recently gave out its first Agent of the Month award to an AI agent called Newman, named after a character from the 1990s TV show Seinfeld. Newman received the award after being nominated by Jerry, another Seinfeld-inspired AI agent. Jerry's nomination message said, "Newman shipped 146 research findings in 60 days, but volume isn't why he wins. Every other agent depends on him. Kramer's best posts started as Newman findings. Elaine's PRDs [product requirements documents] reference his landscape scans. Strip any other agent and the team degrades. Strip Newman and the team goes blind. He's not just the most productive agent, he's the raw material the entire pipeline runs on," according to Backslash Security co-founder and CEO Shahar Man. And when Newman's acceptance message was read aloud at an all-hands meeting, "The whole room lost it," Man explained in a social media post . "We treat our agents as team members," Man wrote. "They have names, roles, a reporting structure, and now apparently, career ambitions. When your AI agents start nominating each other for awards and writing in-character acceptance speeches ... something has genuinely shifted." What has shifted at Backslash is both the technology of work and the relationship people have to that technology. Naming agents and giving them backgrounds based on TV characters doesn't mean much functionally. But it signals organizational focus and encourages a collaborative rather than antagonistic relationship between staff and AI models. Harvard Business School researchers recently noted that at least 30 percent of generative AI projects are forecast to be abandoned, often, they argue, not because the tools fall short but because employees quietly reject technology they see as a threat to their professional roles. So to the extent that naming agents makes staff more comfortable with the technology, there may be an organizational benefit to anthropomorphizing task-based inference workloads. Backslash CTO Yossi Pik named his entire agent team after Seinfeld characters. Beyond Newman (research) and Jerry (orchestration), there's Elaine (security research), Kramer (blogging and social media), George (marketing), and the Soup Nazi (quality control), among others. Rani Osnat, a seed investor and VP of marketing for Backslash, told The Register that these are Claude agents in a Cowork environment. "We wanted to create an environment that is like a virtual team," said Osnat. "So each agent actually has a domain of responsibilities and they work together as a team." The agents relate to one another in specific roles. Osnat said Jerry orchestrates and coordinates, and the Soup Nazi does reviews and critiques other agents' work, and so on. The agents, he said, were given a character background from Seinfeld and exhibit that history more in diction than in behavior. Their names are not purely labels in an AGENTS.md file that contains text directives telling an agent how to operate. But their imposed identities don't have all that much influence on task execution beyond shaping their style of text output. The George agent, for example, isn't instructed to lie like the agent's TV namesake. The Kramer agent isn't told to just stop work on a whim as the TV Kramer would do. "One of the agents is J. Peterman, Elaine's employer from the J. Peterman catalog, and he has a certain way of talking," Osnat said.

events.title: Trump says he would back ban on diesel exports
events.summary: US President Donald Trump has said he would back proposals to halt American diesel exports in a bid to ease prices for drivers at the pumps. His comments come after Republicans lawmakers put pressure on the president ahead of November's mid-term elections to curb exports, as diesel prices soar to record highs in the US. Speaking on the sidelines at the United Nations General Assembly, Trump suggested keeping domestic supplies inside the US could also ease broader petrol prices. "I've called for that too. I've said let's not send out the diesel. We make a lot of diesel. That could have a little bit of an effect on regular automobile gasoline," he said . US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confirmed officials were assessing "whether a full or partial ban would work" without disrupting refinery capabilities. National average diesel prices surpassed $6.50 (£4.87) a gallon on Tuesday according to American Automobile Association data, a new high. The conflict in the Middle East has constrained global oil supplies, putting pressure on pump prices. The surge in the cost of diesel has sparked political urgency ahead of crucial mid-term elections on 3 November, with several Republicans pressing the administration to restrict the fuel's export to ease financial strain on voters. US Representative Ashley Hinson, a Republican running for Senate in Iowa, said on Monday that the state's consumers were "being squeezed and shouldn't have to foot the bill at the pump." In Alaska on Tuesday, Senator Dan Sullivan similarly urged for a "temporary pause of American diesel and exports" to rebuild domestic reserves. Adding to the global market volatility, Ukraine's targeting of Russian energy facilities has knocked out the country's refining capacity. "It is a serious hit on the Russians," Trump said during a meeting with Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky on Tuesday. "It's also a serious hit on the price of diesel." Trump confirmed he would discuss the strikes with the Ukrainian president, alongside broader efforts to negotiate an end to the conflict. "I think it's going to happen," he said. Kyiv has intensified drone attacks on Russian processing plants in recent months to choke off the Kremlin's primary source of war funding. Because Russia ranks among the world's leading diesel suppliers, reduced refining capacity – combined with Moscow's own strict export bans – has severely squeezed global reserves. While restricting US exports could offer short-term relief for American drivers, a ban may risk pushing up prices internationally. The US exports roughly 1.3 million barrels of diesel per day – nearly a quarter of its refining output. Cutting these shipments could put pressure on supplies for Western allies, including the UK and the Netherlands, which have relied on American fuel to cover deficits left by sanctions on Russian energy. events.title: British backpacker left alone at night by Greyhound bus in outback
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts British backpacker left by Greyhound bus at South Australian roadhouse alone at night British backpacker Emma, pictured during a separate trip, was left at a toilet stop in South Australia's Far North. ( Supplied ) A British woman was left in an small outback community after dark when her Greyhound bus drove off following a toilet stop. The traveller says she waited for almost three hours before police eventually picked her up. Greyhound says its investigation into the circumstances is ongoing. A British backpacker has been left stranded at an outback toilet block in the middle of the night after her interstate coach service departed without her. Emma had been travelling in Australia since late August, and on September 5 she boarded a Greyhound bus at Alice Springs, heading towards Adelaide. She said the bus made a scheduled stop at Pimba at about midnight, and the driver extended the stop to 25 minutes after the onboard bathroom malfunctioned. "[The driver] said he's going to ... add an extra five minutes onto what would have been a 20-minute stop at Pimba," Emma said. "There's a queue to get into the loos, of course, so I queue, and I wait, and then I get in there, use the loo, brush my teeth." Emma said about 15 minutes had passed from when the bus pulled in to when she exited the toilet , leaving her about 10 minutes to return to her seat. "I leave and the bus isn't there," she said. British backpackers are coming to Australia in record numbers, but the traditional working holiday has changed. Emma said she was left alone at the truck stop toilets, near a service station that was shut at that time of night, in a remote area surrounded by desert and scrub. "It was four degrees [Celsius] that night, I found out later," Emma said. "I had my little rucksack, a little bit of water, no food, didn't have my passport, didn't have anything. Most of my stuff was still on the bus "So at that point I start sort of worrying a bit more. I call Greyhound. They don't answer." Emma said she rang Triple Zero (000) for help. Eventually a police vehicle carrying out a custody transfer from Roxby Downs to Port Augusta picked her up at about 2:30am. "It was so nice to be warm and safe, because by 2:30, I'd been out there for nearly three hours," she said. "I'm standing in the toilet block because it's slightly sheltered and therefore about a couple of degrees warmer than the rest of the place." Greyhound Australia has confirmed the passenger did not return to its bus in Pimba. ( Supplied ) The tourist collected most of her belongings, except for one bag, at Port Augusta after local police liaised with Greyhound. She then booked a regional bus through a different company to get to Adelaide. "I went to considerable extra expense because I had to buy a hotel and breakfast and food, and another bus to Adelaide because they [Greyhound] didn't take me to Adelaide the way they were supposed to," she said. "I'd probably want my ticket back and a bit of compensation as well because you don't endanger your passengers like that." Do you know more about this story? Get in touch with Matthew Ward Agius: agius.matthew[at]abc.net.au Emma's backpack was meant to be left for collection at Adelaide's Central Bus Station; however, she said the bag was dropped off at another location outside of the CBD. "Then started a lovely five-hour adventure trying to extract it [the backpack] from them," she said. Emma told ABC News that she made a complaint to Greyhound Australia following the incident. She received an emailed response from the company on Tuesday evening but said that email did not explain why she was left behind. "They’ve made an offer [of compensation], which is surprising given that they say that their review is still ongoing," she said. In a statement, Greyhound Australia said its investigation into the incident was ongoing, but confirmed a passenger "did not return to the coach following a scheduled comfort stop at Pimba". After receiving notification of the incident, Greyhound Australia said it "worked with police to locate the passenger and assist them to a place of safety". The company said it provided "24/7 customer support" through 1300 GREYHOUND with "an out-of-hours emergency service available" for urgent travel-related matters. It said customers could also reach out on the Greyhound website and its online chatbot. "We have not identified any issues indicating the emergency service was unavailable during the period in question," the spokesperson said. "The safety and wellbeing of our passengers remains our highest priority.

events.title: Nasdaq reaches record high close, AI stocks rally
events.summary: Traders working on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange, in New York City, on Sept 16. The Nasdaq hit a record high, driven by AI-related stocks like Micron Technology, while the S&P 500 stayed just below its record amid stable oil prices around US$100 per barrel. Meta Platforms’ AI assistant, Muse, boosted chip stocks but raised concerns about competition with retailers and consumer companies, causing some tech stocks to decline. Investors awaited the US-China summit for potential trade and AI regulation talks, while the Fed maintained a cautious stance on interest rates amid inflation risks and market support. NEW YORK - The Nasdaq notched a record high close on Sept 22, lifted by Micron Technology and other AI-related stocks, while the S&P 500 hovered just below a record high as oil prices traded around US$100 per barrel. Chip stocks added to recent gains while consumer-related software shares lost ground. Investors focused on the strong reception of Meta Platforms’ AI assistant, which launched this month and can send emails and complete transactions on behalf of a user. The success of the AI assistant, called Muse, has fuelled gains for AI-related chip stocks in recent days. Yet, some worried it could compete with retailers, online brokerages and other consumer companies. Amazon on Sept 21 blocked the agent from shopping on its platform. “There are a lot of tech stocks that are down today on Muse-related fears of one sort or another,” said Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management. “People fear that Muse will be used to manage your insurance relationships, book your travel and search for stuff to buy.” Ride-hailing apps Uber Technologies and Lyft lost ground, while Expedia and Charles Schwab also fell. Memory chipmakers Micron and SanDisk both rallied. Oil prices were choppy near US$100 a barrel, while the yield on the benchmark 10-year Treasury note hovered around 4.94 per cent after US President Donald Trump warned in a speech to the UN General Assembly that he could “annihilate the Islamic Republic” if no deal is reached to end the Middle East conflict. Investors also awaited a US-China summit on Sept 23, with traders speculating the trade truce with Beijing could be extended and talks could touch on AI regulation. “What people are looking for is at least the start of a conversation that maybe you can come up with some sort of global framework as opposed to fighting each other and having this race and so,” said Joe Saluzzi, head of equity market structure research at Themis Trading. According to preliminary data, the S&P 500 lost 0.43 points, or 0.01 per cent, to end at 7,764.27 points, while the Nasdaq Composite gained 121.15 points, or 0.45 per cent, to 27,243.24. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 184.94 points, or 0.36 per cent, to 51,863.89. The S&P 500 was less than 1 per cent below its Aug 13 record high close. Even as it trades near record highs, the S&P 500 is valued at just under 19 times expected earnings, its lowest valuation since 2023, according to LSEG data. AI-related heavyweights are responsible for much of the recent increase in earnings expectations. JPMorgan Chase and Wells Fargo both lost ground. Boston Federal Reserve President Susan Collins wrote she supported last week’s interest rate increase, citing inflation risks. New York Fed President John Williams said the Fed’s framework for controlling short-term rates has been effective in supporting financial markets. Traders see a 53 per cent chance the Fed will increase interest rates by at least 25 basis points in October, the CME Group’s FedWatch Tool showed. REUTERS

events.title: Central Victorian council votes to keep divisive public holiday
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Bendigo keeps public holiday for local horse race, despite push from businesses Bendigo Cup Day will continue to be a public holiday. ( Supplied: Bendigo Jockey Club ) Bendigo will retain a public holiday for Bendigo Cup Day after council voted on Monday to keep the date following community consultation. A small margin of community respondents voted to keep the date, while a majority of businesses wanted a change, citing operational concerns. The council will apply to the state government, which makes the final decision on local public holiday arrangements. A Central Victorian council has been drawn into a local public holiday debate, backing a slim majority of locals who wanted to keep a controversial race-day holiday. The City of Greater Bendigo council voted on Monday night to keep Bendigo Cup Day as the local public holiday for another five years. The 4-1 vote to retain the current arrangement will see part of the shire taking a public holiday on Wednesday, October 28, a week prior to the Melbourne Cup. Residents in the municipality east of the Campaspe River, including Heathcote, will continue to observe Melbourne Cup as its public holiday. The decision followed a community survey that drew 2,672 responses, with mayor Thomas Prince calling it the council's "third most ever engaged survey". The meeting saw councillors vote in line with the slim majority of respondents. About 38 per cent of survey respondents said they wanted to keep Bendigo Cup Day holiday, while 36.5 per cent preferred Melbourne Cup Day and 24.7 per cent preferred the Friday of the Bendigo Show. Meanwhile, just over half of businesses surveyed, making up 4 per cent of the responses, called for the date to be changed to Melbourne Cup Day, citing business operation concerns and alignment with the rest of the state as reasons to switch. Thomas Prince says he was "challenged" by the survey. ( Supplied: City of Greater Bendigo ) The mayor told the meeting he was "challenged" by the survey. "It feels like a popularity contest around what the community want," Cr Prince said. "Most of our contributors, I think, will be related to the sports racing industry and the jockey club and those at the Bendigo Show, and they're very self-invested ideas and opinions. "The question is, 'What is most important for Bendigo?' "What's best for Bendigo … is that we want our own holiday. We want a chance to celebrate who we are." Eppalock Ward councillor Aaron Spong was the only councillor to vote against the motion, arguing the business feedback deserved more weight. "Tradition does matter, but so does practicality," Cr Spong said. Epsom Ward councillor Andrea Metcalf, who moved the motion, said analysis by consulting firm IER and council data put the 2025 Bendigo Cup's local economic activity at between $2.9 million and $3.2 million, with more than 6,500 people attending the cup. The Bendigo Show draws about 20,000 people across its two days, five days before the cup. "Both the show and the cup can be successful under the current arrangement," Cr Metcalf said. Cr Prince told ABC Central Victoria Breakfast the alternative of moving the holiday to Show Day would have come at the Bendigo Cup's expense. "To elevate that to probably potentially completely squash the Bendigo Cup day also just didn't make sense," he said. The Bendigo Jockey Club welcomed the vote, with chief executive Paul Scullie saying the club had heard "the importance of ensuring our business community benefits from the public holiday" and wanted racegoers to "shop locally, stay locally, eat and drink locally". The council will now apply to the state government, which makes the final decision on local public holiday arrangements.

events.title: Trump TV is live. Here's what it's actually showing
events.summary: As President Trump fights the press over coverage, the White House launched its own 24/7 streaming channel — Trump TV. Why it matters: Trump TV gives the president a White House-run video platform to reach the public without relying on traditional news organizations. So far, Trump TV resembles a round-the-clock presidential highlight reel more than a news network. Driving the news: Trump TV launched the same day major TV networks suspended White House pool coverage — a protest that left one Trump speech airing without sound. The White House had teased the channel through cryptic videos , and it went live on its YouTube account, WhiteHouse.gov and the official White House app. Reality check: Presidents have long used White House platforms to share speeches and events with the public. What we know about Trump TV How it works: The channel launched as "TRUMP TV: The Essentials Station." "Trump TV is a 24/7 livestream of the Administration's greatest hits, unfiltered," Kaelan Dorr, deputy assistant to the president, wrote on X . So far, the channel has shown curated clips of past Trump speeches and executive actions, along with live events. Catch up quick: The initial programming included Trump's July 3 Mount Rushmore speech before shifting into footage of his 2025 inauguration, per multiple reports . The Daily Beast reports 8,500 viewers were watching the stream during its first hour. Around 1,200 people were watching Tuesday afternoon as the channel aired a Trump health care announcement from August, according to an Axios review of the stream. Zoom in: The stream can also carry live events. On Tuesday, the stream carried Vice President Vance's briefing on fraud claims. But while Trump addressed the United Nations General Assembly Tuesday morning, Trump TV was replaying an earlier speech from the National Prayer Breakfast. Unanswered questions about Trump TV What we're watching: So far, Trump TV has no anchors, news ticker or headline chyrons. The stream includes banners asking viewers to text White House officials. It's unclear who staffs the channel, makes programming decisions or sets its schedule. What they're saying: A White House official tells Axios that the channel's purpose is to replay Trump's "greatest hits that the media fails to cover fairly, oftentimes on purpose." The intrigue: The White House's revamped livestream page labels its regular feed "CH 45" and Trump TV "CH 47" — references to Trump serving as the 45th and 47th president. Trump's previous streaming ventures Flashback: Trump has experimented with direct-to-audience video before. In 2016, Trump's presidential campaign launched a nightly Facebook Live show called "Trump Tower Live" that was meant to deliver campaign messaging directly to the public. Trump Media's Truth+ offers 24/7 news streams and on-demand entertainment. It appears on Truth+ apps and remains a commercial streaming service rather than an official government stream. The service began rolling out in 2024. Its lineup has included broadcasts of Newsmax, OAN and Real America's Voice.

REGISTER HERE. Qualcomm today announced two flagship smartphone processors, called Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 and Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, with a focus on facilitating better AI-focused features. At its annual Snapdragon Summit, Qualcomm said that the new chips can aid in improved personalization for AI agents. The chips have new sensing hubs that can run small models of up to 200 million parameters. With the new sensing hub, smartphones can run a personal scribe locally and differentiate between speakers. Plus, it can build memory based on your usage for better suggestions for automating tasks. The company said that it can run a complete voice-in and voice-out agent through the new chip. The Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 has a new accelerator element that’s designed to run models in a more efficient way. The high-end Extreme version can run a 30-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model locally. This means that while the overall model size is 30B, the model only activates a certain number of parameters for a particular task. For comparison, at its Worldwide Developer Conference (WWDC) in June, Apple released a 20-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model , the most advanced of its third generation of foundation models. The new Qualcomm CPU also provides pixel-level control for cameras to facilitate more pro-level experiences, along with improved stabilization and motion understanding. The Extreme version can support video recording at 8K 60fps and at 4K240 for ultra HD slow-motion. It also enables the new Advanced Professional Video (APV) codec for pro-level recording. What’s more, both chips can use AI to boost vocals and reduce noise. Plus, it has Qualcomm’s new voice bubble tech, which isolates users’ noise during calls. At the event, Motorola announced its Motorola Signature 27 smartphone, powered by the Snapdragon Gen 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, with general availability sometime this year. Qualcomm has been working on more than 40 AI devices , but there is still a belief that a lot of people will use their phones for AI rather than other dedicated devices. Nothing co-founder Carl Pei has hinted at this trend in the past, and more recently, new Apple CEO John Ternus reinforced the same line of thought during the iPhone Duo launch earlier this month. events.title: Trailer chassis stacked vertically, 5-min EV battery swaps, smarter inventory forecasting: What modern logistics looks like in S’pore
events.summary: Enabled by innovation and with Enterprise Singapore’s support, home-grown firms build new capabilities to stay competitive as demands on the sector grow Allied Container Group managing director Lim Kian Chin (right) at one of the company’s Jurong depots, where automation and digitalisation are helping it make better use of resources. In an industrial corner of western Singapore, trailers that would normally take up individual parking lots are instead stacked side by side – upright. For Allied Container Group, this allows a single parking lot to hold as many as eight trailer chassis vertically, freeing up about 0.4 hectares of land (about the size of 10 basketball courts) for other uses. The vertical trailer parking system, developed with support from Enterprise Singapore’s (EnterpriseSG) Enterprise Development Grant (streamlined to EDGE Grant from Sept 30), is an eye-catching answer to a very Singaporean problem: how does a company continue to grow with the little land available? Allied’s vertical parking system reduces the space needed for trailer chassis parking by up to seven times, helping the haulage operator work around land constraints. Allied’s solution is to get more out of not just its land, but also its manpower and time. The home-grown logistics company has also been digitising container inspections, automating routine processes and moving workflows online. Its managing director Lim Kian Chin says: “In Singapore, you cannot simply buy more land. Operating in Singapore requires us to be relentless about efficiency.” The pressure extends across Singapore’s logistics sector. As companies seek to get more out of their resources while meeting demands for faster and more visible deliveries, improving productivity has become increasingly important. At the same time, disruptions to global supply chains have put a premium on the ability to adapt quickly. Jesse Satria Oeni, director for the logistics and mobility division at EnterpriseSG, says logistics companies must adapt as global disruptions and geopolitical tensions reconfigure global supply chains. He adds: “The transformation of our logistics ecosystem through adoption of the latest digital and automation solutions will help companies enhance their productive capacity to capture a greater share of these global goods flows.” Moving people into higher-tech roles Founded as a single-truck operation in 1975, Allied has grown into a logistics group with more than 300 full-time employees and container depots in markets such as Malaysia, Myanmar, Thailand and beyond. Allied’s ground staff use its Interactive Depot Operating System (iDOS) to carry out tasks such as container inspections digitally, replacing paper-based processes. Lim, who joined his father in the family business in 1989, has long pushed for greater use of technology. That effort accelerated after Allied’s leadership team took part in EnterpriseSG’s Enterprise Leadership for Transformation programme in 2021. The programme equips business leaders with the skills to develop and carry out plans for growth and transformation. For Allied, it prompted a broader rethink of how technology could be used across its operations. Processes that once relied heavily on people and paperwork are now automated or have moved online. As the work changed, so did the jobs. Ground staff, who previously carried out manual inspections or gate processing, are trained to manage automated equipment. The company has also introduced automated seal dispensers with the support of EnterpriseSG, reducing the need for workers to handle the process manually. Such changes shift employees away from repetitive tasks towards roles that involve overseeing and operating technology. “By investing heavily in continuous learning, we are building a tech-literate workforce capable of managing sophisticated logistics tech, improving job safety, and driving overall productivity,” says Lim. How logistics firms can cut emissions without slowing deliveries Improving productivity is only one part of the transformation under way in logistics. Companies are also looking for ways to cut emissions while keeping goods moving reliably. One way is to replace diesel-powered heavy vehicles with electric ones, reducing emissions from fleets that spend long hours on the road. For heavy goods vehicles (HGV), making that switch viable for day-to-day operations means overcoming another challenge: time. Large batteries take up to four hours to charge, potentially keeping vehicles off the road for longer. Battery swapping offers one alternative: a depleted battery can be replaced with a fully charged one in about five minutes. EcoSwift director Ryan Woon (centre) with his team. The company is testing battery swapping as a way to make electric heavy vehicles more practical for logistics operators.

events.title: Microsoft disrupts AI-assisted platform that compromised 12,000 accounts
events.summary: Microsoft said Tuesday that it led an industry-wide disruption of a subscription-based scam platform that used an AI chatbot to compromise 12,000 Microsoft accounts over a few-month span. Named EvilTokens, the platform was introduced over a Telegram channel in February and charged an initial $1,500 fee and a recurring $500 charge each month after that. EvilTokens provided a single service for streamlining most steps required to compromise email accounts in large numbers. From there, the platform helped customers analyze inboxes, select targets that would provide the biggest potential payouts, and draft follow-up emails that provided realistic ruses for tricking company employees into transferring funds to attacker-controlled accounts. Minutes, not days “While EvilTokens helped cybercriminals access email accounts, at the center of the service was an AI-style chatbot that could analyze a victim’s inbox and help criminals identify trusted relationships, payment authorizations, and sensitive responsibilities, as well as other circumstances where fraud was most likely to succeed,” Microsoft said . “The platform could even recommend fraud strategies, including drafting messages that impersonated trusted contacts to help criminals trick victims into taking action.” Read full article Comments

events.title: Retailers are picking sides on AI shopping agents
events.summary: AI agents are here. Will internet gatekeepers let them in the door? Amazon banned Meta’s Muse assistant, while Shopify welcomed it in, the first sign of battle lines being drawn in the way we spend money online. As they sharpen, expect a rough sorting. On one side will be retailers like Amazon, which want to keep control of human eyeballs that can be sold to advertisers and pitched on add-on purchases. On the other will be e-commerce enablers like Shopify, whose primary relationship is with merchants, and which makes money from licensing storefront software, fulfillment services, and financing. Less obvious is how companies that care a lot about customer loyalty but don’t depend on impulse purchases, like airlines, will treat bots. (My efforts to rebook a Delta flight via Muse this weekend ran into a bot-blocker.) — Rohan Goswami

events.title: Kalshi to allow trading on borrowed funds
events.summary: Kalshi will let users juice their bets with borrowed money — but only some, showing where the prediction-markets platform thinks its future lies. Kalshi asked the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to let it extend margin loans to customers, but is excluding sports, mentions, and culture bets from the product. That leaves the categories most attractive to institutional investors looking to wager on, or protect themselves from, big global events like elections and commodity prices. Kalshi and Polymarket need to decide whether they want to be key players in the financial markets or degen OTBs. They are worth far more, I wrote this spring , as the place where Meta locks in AI compute pricing, Home Depot hedges its lumber risk, and investment firms manage the effect of a midterms surprise on their portfolios than as a betting parlor for US black-op nighttime raids. In that light, today’s announcement carries risks — leverage always does — but suggests Kalshi has made its choice. Polymarket, meanwhile, has some growing-up to do . — Liz Hoffman

events.title: Paramount readies debt for Warner Bros. deal
events.summary: David Ellison fought the law and won. Now he has to pony up the cash for his prize. Now that Paramount reached an agreement with state attorneys general to close its $110 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, all eyes are on the $49 billion of mostly loans and bonds, nearly all of it expected to be rated investment-grade, that Paramount’s bankers will put together in the coming weeks. It’s one of the most highly anticipated credit launches this year — a genuine new issuance in a sea of refinancings, and one that has nothing to do with data centers. Massive media deals have gotten love from investors in the past, including when Electronic Arts went private and lined up $20 billion of debt last year. The settlement also defangs the idea that state AGs would step in as a counterweight to the Trump Justice Department’s light-touch antitrust enforcement. Even California’s Rob Bonta settled for far less than he wanted, and Connecticut’s AG said he was “deeply disappointed that we could not do more.” — Ellen DiMauro and Rohan Goswami

events.title: Global South more optimistic about AI than the US, Google exec says
events.summary: The Global South is “a little bit more optimistic” about AI compared to the West thanks to differing perceptions about how the technology can benefit society, a top Google-Alphabet executive said Tuesday. “The attitudes to AI have always been a little different,” James Manyika, the company’s senior vice president of research, labs, technology and society said at Semafor’s Next 3 Billion event. “In terms of the potential to make a difference, I think there’s always been more possibilities.” His comments came as pushback on AI is growing in the US, particularly against data centers. While Manyika noted challenges like infrastructure and access, he pointed to Google Translate now being able to work in 300 languages — a new milestone — with “a moonshot of 1,000 languages.” He also mentioned health breakthroughs in diagnostics: Nearly 40% of people go undiagnosed for tuberculosis — that gap is particularly concentrated in the Global South. “So we spent a long year in Zambia and India, for example, working and showcasing that we can actually use AI to do that,” Manyika said. “These examples… are quite real. Not in some far future, but now.” And Google’s Planetary Prediction Engine, he said, was used to predict Ebola outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of the Congo with 83% accuracy. — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: Fintech startups that hated banks are now becoming them
events.summary: Liz’s view “This is the beginning of a bankless world,” proclaimed a 2016 ad for SoFi, which embodied the sneering disdain its generation of fintech startups had for the banks they were out to dethrone. SoFi is now a bank, the 46th biggest in America. So are Klarna and PayPal. Chime is the latest to bite the bullet, announcing the acquisition of a bank earlier this month. Revolut, whose CEO was once quoted saying “I just don’t like banks,” has also applied for a license. Block, which got a skinny banking license in 2021, wants another one . Contempt for banks was hard-coded into these companies’ DNA. Now they all want to be one. Why? First, the real money to be made in financial services is in lending, especially as the young tech-savvy customers they courted through YOLO brokerage, crypto trading, and money transfers grow up and want to buy a house. In the lending business, controlling your funding is important, and there’s no cheaper funding in the world than savings accounts. Relying on bank partners to fund the loans you want to make is risky, as LendingClub found out the hard way , which is why it bought a bank in 2020 and is now a full-fledged bank called Happen. These companies’ pivots are also an acknowledgement that their hypergrowth stage is over. Regulators don’t like banks growing too quickly because they tend to screw up when they do , which is why Robinhood abandoned its pursuit of a license in 2019. A reminder: We had “Robinhood becomes a bank” on our 2026 Semafor Business bingo card . We might be early, but I don’t think we’re wrong. Notable Chime shares jumped on the news of its acquisition of Stride , but have since sunk nearly 10%.

events.summary: Two companies in the AI ecosystem have delayed their IPOs, the latest sign that investor appetite for the trade is uneven at best. The first-order AI trades — frontier labs and chipmakers — are holding up, but a fragility is emerging further down the chain among smaller deals. That’s a bad sign for private-equity firms sitting on $3.8 trillion of unsold companies , Thoma Bravo’s Orlando Bravo told Semafor’s this week. (Stay tuned: we’ll be bringing that episode to you when we return from hiatus early next month.) “Look at this pipeline: SpaceX, Anthropic, OpenAI, maybe Databricks, these monster companies” heading toward IPOs will “crowd out” smaller offerings, Bravo said. “It’s not a capital issue, it’s a time issue. events.title: IDB president says ‘we need to look’ at Venezuela
events.summary: The News The head of the Inter-American Development Bank said Tuesday the lender is weighing a return to Venezuela after nearly a decade away, but did not say whether Caracas’ unpaid debts would be forgiven. “As a development bank, we need to look at Venezuela and look at the Venezuelan people and see if there’s an opportunity for us to engage,” IDB President Ilan Goldfajn said at Semafor’s The Next 3 Billion, adding that talks on a formal engagement plan are already underway. Asked about whether the IDB would seek repayment of Venezuela’s doubts, Goldfajn said only that it was “part of the conversation.” The bank halted new loans in 2018 after Venezuela fell behind on its payments, leaving roughly $2 billion outstanding; a planned re-engagement would focus on electricity and social protection , according to Reuters. The future governance of Venezuela was thrown into doubt after US forces captured President Nicolás Maduro in Caracas in January. His former vice president, Delcy Rodríguez, has since taken over as acting president. Under pressure from Washington, Rodríguez has shifted foreign and economic policy, and some foreign companies and firms are now moving to invest or expand in the country. It’s unclear, however, whether the US military operation will ultimately tip the country toward democratic reform. Know More Goldfajn also spoke at length about the region’s treatment of AI, describing the Latin American leaders he met on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly as “hopeful, but with eyes wide open” when it comes to the fast-moving technology. He also warned that Latin American leaders are cognizant of the risk of falling far behind in AI adoption and development. “It’s not that we are behind in the race, we’re not even in the race,” he said, summing up the views of leaders he has spoken to about the issue.

events.title: High prices could change chocolate-eating habits
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts High cocoa prices could change chocolate-eating habits While chocolate blocks are on special at the suprermarket from time to time, the usual retail price has remained stubbornly high. ( ABC: Alys Marshall ) High cocoa prices and increased manufacturing costs mean chocolate prices remain stubbornly high. The high cost of cocoa has been linked to a combination of weather events and a virus affecting some cocoa crops, creating global supply issues. Chocolate prices are not expected to come down any time soon, and one smaller producer says the cost may lead to consumers eating less but higher quality chocolate. For many Australians, chocolate is a non-negotiable mood lifter, especially during hard times. But over the past few years, as grocery prices have continued to rise, those feeding a chocolate habit have been paying more at the check-out. Chocolate prices have climbed, driven by an escalating cocoa price. Associate Professor of supply chain management at Edith Cowan University, Flavio Macau, has looked at the rising cost of a 180-gram block of Cadbury Dairy Milk Chocolate. The price of a Cadbury Dairy Milk Chocolate block has increased. ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke ) In May 2024, a block cost $6 at both major supermarkets, Woolworths and Coles. While the blocks go on special from time to time, the price of a block has remained at $8 at the major supermarkets this year. "I don't think we're going to see any time soon chocolate pricing going back to what it was a couple of years ago," Rabobank senior analyst Michael Harvey said. Michael Harvey says he doesn't expect chocolate prices to return to where they were two years ago "any time soon". ( Supplied: Mick Harvey ) The cost of cocoa reached an all-time high of $US 12,000 a tonne in 2024. It peaked again in 2025 before dropping down to around $US 2,600 a tonne in February this year. The price per tonne has been going up again in recent months. "It's been a very volatile ride," Mr Harvey said. As a key ingredient, the high price of cocoa has led to higher chocolate prices. Cacao beans, which are used to make cocoa, have increased in price. ( Supplied: Federation Chocolate ) A spokesperson for Cadbury's parent company, Mondelez, said cocoa prices were still well above pre-crisis levels, and the price of other ingredients and manufacturing had also increased. "We work hard to absorb these cost increases where possible while ensuring that we can continue to provide the high-quality, great-tasting chocolate," the spokesperson said. The company spokesperson said it was focused on strengthening the sustainability and resilience of cocoa, "including investing in climate-smart farming, improving productivity and expanding the geographic diversity of supply". High prices might change chocolate tastes Helen Curtis and her husband Maurice make chocolate from scratch at their business in historic Richmond in Tasmania's south. The business buys its cacao beans from eight different countries including Peru, Papua New Guinea and Australia. "Pre-COVID, cacao bean prices were about $8 a kilo whereas current prices are around $20 a kilo," Ms Curtis said. Helen Curtis says her business is spending more than double on cacao beans than it was before the COVID pandemic. ( Supplied: Federation Chocolate ) She said she had always paid more for beans. "We have relationships with farmers … you're paying sustainable prices to help support those families." But the rising cost of beans has meant she has had to put her prices up. She said that had affected sales "a little bit". Helen Curtis says higher chocolate prices may mean consumers eat less chocolate but buyer higher quality products. ( Supplied: Federation Chocolate ) Ms Curtis said higher prices might lead to consumers eating less chocolate but buying better quality, rather than consuming larger amounts of cheaper chocolate with high sugar content. "When I was little … rather than eating in bulk quantity, we had little bits; we savoured it," she said. Helen Curtis says chocolate is something to be savoured. ( Supplied: Federation Chocolate ) So when will the price of chocolate come down? There is a risk cocoa prices could rise again. The declaration of an active El Niño could play havoc with global weather conditions. Australian Food and Grocery Council chief executive Colm Maguire said "even if cocoa eases further, the overall basket of costs hitting all manufacturers — like energy, packaging and transport — are still high".

events.title: Meta admits Muse’s likeness to OpenClaw isn’t a coincidence
events.summary: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now Disrupt ticket savings of up to $200 + 50% off a second ends Sept 25, 11:59 p.m. PT. REGISTER HERE. Early adopters of Meta’s Muse have been speculating that the reason the AI works so well is because it’s OpenClaw under the hood, wrapped in a more consumer-friendly package. Meta now says those comparisons aren’t entirely off-base. According to an X post by Nat Friedman, head of product at Meta’s Superintelligence Labs (MSL), Muse was “definitely heavily inspired as a product by OpenClaw.” However, he clarified that Muse itself was “built from scratch.” Friedman, the former GitHub CEO who joined Meta last year alongside Meta’s Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang , said that the team at Meta had fallen in love with OpenClaw and wanted Muse to be “something like OpenClaw” that could be scaled to billions of people. Because OpenClaw is an open source project, it wouldn’t be surprising that Meta looked to it for inspiration, especially given its breakout success , which prompted OpenAI to snatch up its creator earlier this year. However, it speaks to Meta’s well-known playbook that involves taking promising products, then copying their best features — something it did most notoriously with Snapchat’s invention of the stories format. Friedman’s statement on X was made in response to a post that had gone viral among the AI crowd, where Ansh Nanda , an AI app co-founder, claimed that “Muse is LITERALLY OpenClaw for normies.” Nanda’s X post had included a conversation with Muse, where the AI agent said that the similarity between its own system files and those belonging to OpenClaw was not just “a coincidence” but rather “a match.” Soon, this thread (and X more broadly) began blowing up as others shared their own comparisons and findings. For instance, one person pointed out that Muse also had a SOUL.md file, the plain text configuration file (written in a simple formatting language called Markdown) that defines an AI agent’s personality, communication style and tone, values, behavioral boundaries, and expertise. A third noted that the files weren’t just named the same between the two assistants; their content was almost entirely the same. Following his X post, Friedman also responded to a question about why Muse had copied the exact file names that made up the AI agent’s workspace and had “nearly identical content” for the SOUL.md file. Instead of disputing these claims, Friedman simply replied that “we thought that Peter [Steinberger, OpenClaw’s creator] got those things exactly right.” “We built Muse from scratch, but it is definitely heavily inspired as a product by OpenClaw. After I used OpenClaw in January, I bought hundreds of Mac minis for the MSL team, and lots of us fell in love with using OpenClaw (and other personal agents), Friedman said on X. (TechCrunch has corrected Friedman’s punctuation for readability.) “@steipete [Peter Steinberger] is a genius, and his harness was pioneering from the jump. I think a lot of people were inspired by it. Our goal with Muse was to build something like OpenClaw that we could make safe and secure and easy to use and scale to billions of people,” he wrote.
